records.title: Change in Tandem
records.text:
Change in Tandem
How input values and output values of a function vary together: domain and range, increasing and decreasing, concavity, and zeros.
A function is a rule that relates two changing quantities. Describing how the output values change as the input values change, whether they increase or decrease and whether the rate of change is increasing or decreasing, is the starting point for every function in this course.
Unit 1 is built on two ideas: covariation, meaning how output values change in tandem with input values, and rates of change. This topic is about the first idea, and it introduces the precise language the AP Exam expects whenever you describe a function.
records.excerpt: How input values and output values of a function vary together: domain and range, increasing and decreasing, concavity, and zeros.

records.title: Change in Tandem
records.heading: 1.1.A · A function maps each input value to exactly one output value.
records.text:
1.1.A · A function maps each input value to exactly one output value.
Each input value has exactly one output value. Images are output values, and preimages are sets of input values.
A function is a mathematical relation that maps a set of input values to a set of output values such that each input value is mapped to exactly one output value. The set of input values is called the domain of the function, and the set of output values is called the range of the function. The variable representing input values is called the independent variable, and the variable representing output values is called the dependent variable.
Values of the function f

Different input values may share an output value, as 0 and 1 do above. One input value with two output values is not allowed. The image of an input value is the single output value yielded by the function rule. Since f(0) = 3, the image of 0 is 3. The preimage of an output value is the set of input values for which the function rule yields that output value. Here, the preimage of 3 is {0, 1}.
Two functions f and g are equal only when they have the same domain and f(a) = g(a) for every input value a in that domain. A function can be given graphically, numerically (a table), analytically (a formula), or verbally (a description). The representation changes, but the function does not.
Name both variables with their units. For example: The input values of the function h are times, in seconds, and the output values are heights, in feet.

records.title: Change in Tandem
records.heading: 1.1.A · Increasing and decreasing compare output values as input values increase.
records.text:
1.1.A · Increasing and decreasing compare output values as input values increase.
State the interval, then say how the output values change as the input values increase.
A function is increasing over an interval of its domain if, as the input values increase, the output values always increase. That is, for all a and b in the interval, if a < b, then f(a) < f(b). A function is decreasing over an interval of its domain if, as the input values increase, the output values always decrease. That is, for all a and b in the interval, if a < b, then f(a) > f(b).

Comparing function values: from t = 0 to t = 1.5 each output value is greater than the one before, and from t = 1.5 to t = 3 each output value is less than the one before. So h is increasing on the interval 0 < t < 1.5 and decreasing on the interval 1.5 < t < 3.
On the interval 0 < t < 1.5, as t increases, h(t) increases. On the interval 1.5 < t < 3, as t increases, h(t) decreases. Telling open intervals apart from closed intervals when you state where a function is increasing or decreasing is outside the scope of the course, so either form is accepted.

records.text:
1.1.B · Concavity describes whether the rate of change is increasing or decreasing.
Concave up means the rate of change is increasing. Concave down means the rate of change is decreasing.
The graph of a function is concave up on intervals in which the rate of change is increasing, and concave down on intervals in which the rate of change is decreasing. Increasing or decreasing is one question, and concave up or concave down is a separate question.

records.title: Change in Tandem
records.heading: 1.1.B · A zero is an input value where the output value is zero.
records.text:
1.1.B · A zero is an input value where the output value is zero.
A zero is an input value. The output value at a zero is 0.
The graph of a function intersects the x-axis when the output value is zero, and the corresponding input values are the zeros of the function. If p(x) = (x − 2)(x + 5), then p(2) = 0 and p(−5) = 0, so the zeros of p are x = 2 and x = −5, and the graph crosses the x-axis at the points (2, 0) and (−5, 0).
Analytically: set the output equal to 0 and solve.
Numerically: look for table rows whose output value is 0.
Graphically: look for the input values where the graph meets the x-axis.
Verbally: ask when the measured quantity equals 0, such as when a height reaches the ground.
records.excerpt: A zero is an input value. The output value at a zero is 0.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.text:
Rates of Change
Average rates of change over intervals, rates of change at a point, and what the sign of a rate of change says about how two quantities vary together.
Rates of change quantify how two quantities vary together. An average rate of change describes an interval, and average rates of change over smaller and smaller intervals approximate the rate of change at a point.
Topic 1.1 described whether output values increase or decrease. This topic measures how fast they do. Average rate of change, with units and an interpretation, appears in nearly every modeling free-response question on the AP Exam.
records.excerpt: Average rates of change over intervals, rates of change at a point, and what the sign of a rate of change says about how two quantities vary together.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.2.A · The average rate of change is a ratio of changes over an interval.
records.text:
1.2.A · The average rate of change is a ratio of changes over an interval.
Average rate of change = (change in output values)/(change in input values), stated for an interval and with units.
The average rate of change of a function f over the interval a ≤ x ≤ b is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a), the ratio of the change in the output values to the change in the input values. It is the constant rate of change that would give the same change in output values as f gives over that interval. Its units are output units per input unit.
Position s(t), in meters, of a cyclist at time t, in seconds, where s(t) = t² + 5t
t
s(t)
0
0
2
14
5
50
9
126
Over 2 ≤ t ≤ 5 the average rate of change is (s(5) − s(2))/(5 − 2) = (50 − 14)/3 = 12 meters per second. Over 5 ≤ t ≤ 9 it is (126 − 50)/4 = 19 meters per second. The answers differ, so an average rate of change always belongs to a stated interval.
Show the computation, then interpret it with the interval, the direction, and units: (s(5) − s(2))/(5 − 2) = 12. From t = 2 to t = 5 seconds, on average, the position of the cyclist increased at a rate of 12 meters per second.
The average rate of change of s over [2, 5] is the slope of the dashed secant line

records.heading: 1.2.A · Average rates of change over small intervals approximate the rate of change at a point.
records.text:
1.2.A · Average rates of change over small intervals approximate the rate of change at a point.
To estimate the rate of change at a point, use the average rate of change over a small interval containing the point.
The rate of change of a function at a point measures how fast the output values would change if the input values changed at that point. It can be approximated by the average rates of change of the function over small intervals containing the point, if such values exist.

records.heading: 1.2.A · Compare rates of change at two points with small intervals near each point.
records.text:
1.2.A · Compare rates of change at two points with small intervals near each point.
Use intervals of the same small length near each point, then compare the two average rates of change.
The rates of change at two points can be compared using average rates of change over sufficiently small intervals containing each point. Near t = 3 the rate of change of s is about 11 meters per second. Over 7.9 ≤ t ≤ 8.1 the average rate of change is (106.11 − 101.91)/0.2 = 21 meters per second. So the position is changing faster at t = 8 than at t = 3.
Because the average rate of change of s over 7.9 ≤ t ≤ 8.1 is greater than the average rate of change over 2.9 ≤ t ≤ 3.1, the rate of change of s at t = 8 is greater than the rate of change of s at t = 3.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.2.B · The sign of a rate of change describes how two quantities vary together.
records.text:
1.2.B · The sign of a rate of change describes how two quantities vary together.
Interpret a rate of change with its sign, its size, its units, and its interval or point.
A positive rate of change means that as one quantity increases or decreases, the other quantity does the same.
A negative rate of change means that as one quantity increases, the other decreases.
The size of a rate of change tells how much the output values change per unit change in the input values.
A rate of change can be positive at some points and negative at others, and an average rate of change over a long interval can hide those changes. An average rate of change of −0.5 degrees Celsius per minute for cooling coffee means that, on average, the temperature decreased by 0.5 degrees Celsius per minute over that interval. It does not mean the temperature fell at that rate every minute.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.text:
Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
Average rates of change for sequences, linear functions, and quadratic functions, secant lines, and how the change in average rates of change reveals concavity.
The pattern of average rates of change over consecutive equal-length input-value intervals identifies a function type. Constant average rates of change mean linear. Average rates of change that change at a constant rate mean quadratic.
Topic 1.2 computed and interpreted average rates of change. This topic studies how those average rates of change themselves change, which is the reasoning the AP Exam expects when you justify a choice of model from a table.
records.excerpt: Average rates of change for sequences, linear functions, and quadratic functions, secant lines, and how the change in average rates of change reveals concavity.

records.heading: 1.3.A · For a linear function, the average rate of change is constant.
records.text:
1.3.A · For a linear function, the average rate of change is constant.
A linear function has the same average rate of change over every interval.
For a linear function, the average rate of change over any length input-value interval is constant. For f(x) = 3x + 2, every interval gives an average rate of change of 3, the slope of the line.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.heading: 1.3.A · The average rate of change over [a, b] is the slope of a secant line.
records.text:
1.3.A · The average rate of change over [a, b] is the slope of a secant line.
Average rate of change over [a, b] and the slope of the secant line are the same number.
The average rate of change of a function f over the closed interval [a, b] is the slope of the secant line from the point (a, f(a)) to the point (b, f(b)). For f(x) = x², the secant line from (1, 1) to (3, 9) has slope (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4, which is also the average rate of change of f over [1, 3].
Different intervals give secant lines with different slopes unless the function is linear. That is a picture of why only a linear function has a constant average rate of change.
Secant line of f(x) = x² over the interval [1, b], with slope (b² − 1)/(b − 1) = b + 1

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.heading: 1.3.B · The change in the average rates of change reveals concavity.
records.text:
1.3.B · The change in the average rates of change reveals concavity.
Increasing average rates of change mean concave up, and decreasing ones mean concave down.
For a linear function, the average rates of change over consecutive equal-length intervals are given by a constant function, so they change at a rate of zero. For a quadratic function, they are given by a linear function, so they change at a constant rate.
When the average rate of change over equal-length input-value intervals is increasing for all small-length intervals, the graph of the function is concave up. When it is decreasing for all small-length intervals, the graph is concave down.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, extrema between real zeros, and points of inflection.
Where the rate of change of a polynomial function changes sign, the function has a relative maximum or minimum. Where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing, or the reverse, the graph has a point of inflection.
Topics 1.1 to 1.3 described output values and rates of change in general. Polynomial functions are the first family where those ideas combine into several turning points and changes in concavity on one graph.
records.excerpt: Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, extrema between real zeros, and points of inflection.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.4.A · A polynomial function has a degree, a leading term, and a leading coefficient.
records.text:
1.4.A · A polynomial function has a degree, a leading term, and a leading coefficient.
Write the terms from highest to lowest power: the first term is the leading term, and its power is the degree.
A nonconstant polynomial function of x is any function representation equivalent to p(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀, where n is a positive integer, each aᵢ is a real number, and aₙ is nonzero. The polynomial has degree n, the leading term is aₙxⁿ, and the leading coefficient is aₙ.

A product such as x(x − 1)(x + 2) is a polynomial because it is equivalent to x³ + x² − 2x. Expressions such as 5/x or √x are not polynomials, because they are not equivalent to a sum of terms with positive integer powers of x.

records.heading: 1.4.A · Relative extrema occur where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing.
records.text:
1.4.A · Relative extrema occur where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing.
A relative extremum is greatest or least nearby. An absolute extremum is greatest or least over the whole domain.
Where a polynomial function switches between increasing and decreasing, or at an included endpoint of a polynomial with a restricted domain, the function has a local, or relative, maximum or minimum output value. If a relative maximum is greater than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, maximum. If a relative minimum is less than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, minimum.

As x increases from −2 to −1, f(x) increases from −2 to 2, and from −1 to 1, f(x) decreases to −2. So f has a relative maximum of 2 at x = −1 and a relative minimum of −2 at x = 1. Neither is absolute, because a cubic's output values increase without bound in one direction and decrease without bound in the other.
A polynomial function of even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum. For a quadratic function, the global maximum or global minimum occurs at the vertex. Both ends of the graph of an even-degree polynomial point the same way, which is why one of them must exist.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.4.A · Between two distinct real zeros there is a relative extremum.
records.text:
1.4.A · Between two distinct real zeros there is a relative extremum.
Two distinct real zeros guarantee at least one relative extremum between them, not exactly one.
Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function, there must be at least one input value corresponding to a relative maximum or relative minimum. The output values leave 0 and return to 0, so the function must change direction in between.
For g(x) = x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2), with zeros at −2, 0, and 2, technology shows a relative maximum of about 3.079 at x ≈ −1.155 between −2 and 0, and a relative minimum of about −3.079 at x ≈ 1.155 between 0 and 2.

records.text:
1.4.A · Points of inflection occur where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing, or the reverse.
An extremum is a change in direction. A point of inflection is a change in concavity.
Points of inflection of a polynomial function occur at input values where the rate of change of the function changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing. This is where the graph changes from concave up to concave down or from concave down to concave up.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
Zeros and linear factors, multiplicity, complex zeros and conjugates, degree from successive differences, and even and odd functions.
The zeros of a polynomial function, counted with multiplicity, determine its linear factors, where its graph crosses or is tangent to the x-axis, and the endpoints of the intervals where it is positive or negative.
Topic 1.4 showed that relative extrema sit between real zeros. This topic studies the zeros themselves, including non-real zeros that never appear on the graph but still count toward the degree.
records.excerpt: Zeros and linear factors, multiplicity, complex zeros and conjugates, degree from successive differences, and even and odd functions.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: 1.5.A · A real number a is a zero of p if and only if (x − a) is a linear factor of p.
records.text:
1.5.A · A real number a is a zero of p if and only if (x − a) is a linear factor of p.
Real zeros give linear factors, x-intercepts, and the endpoints of the intervals where p(x) > 0 or p(x) < 0.
If a is a complex number and p(a) = 0, then a is a zero of the polynomial function p, or a root of the equation p(x) = 0. If a is a real number, then (x − a) is a linear factor of p if and only if a is a zero of p, and the graph of y = p(x) has an x-intercept at the point (a, 0). For example, p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3), so the real zeros of p are 1, −2, and 3.
Real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints for intervals satisfying polynomial inequalities. To solve p(x) > 0, find the real zeros, then determine the sign of p(x) on each interval between them.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: 1.5.A · A repeated linear factor gives a zero with multiplicity.
records.text:
1.5.A · A repeated linear factor gives a zero with multiplicity.
Even multiplicity: same sign on both sides and tangent to the x-axis. Odd multiplicity: the sign changes and the graph crosses.
If a linear factor (x − a) is repeated n times, the corresponding zero of the polynomial function has a multiplicity n. A polynomial function of degree n has exactly n complex zeros when counting multiplicities. For p(x) = (x + 1)²(x − 2)³, the zero −1 has multiplicity 2, the zero 2 has multiplicity 3, and the degree is 5.
If a real zero a has even multiplicity, then the signs of the output values are the same for input values near x = a, and the graph is tangent to the x-axis at x = a. If a has odd multiplicity, the output values change sign and the graph crosses the x-axis.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: 1.5.A · Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
records.text:
1.5.A · Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, and every zero counts toward the degree.
A complex number has the form a + bi, where a and b are real and i² = −1. If a + bi is a non-real zero of a polynomial function p, then its conjugate a − bi is also a zero of p. For example, x² − 2x + 5 has zeros 1 + 2i and 1 − 2i.
Non-real zeros are not x-intercepts, but they count toward the degree. The function p(x) = (x² + 4)(x − 1) has degree 3 and three complex zeros, 2i, −2i, and 1, but its graph has only one x-intercept, at (1, 0). Because non-real zeros come in pairs, a polynomial of odd degree has at least one real zero.
records.excerpt: Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, and every zero counts toward the degree.

records.heading: 1.5.A · The degree is the least n for which the nth differences are constant.
records.text:
1.5.A · The degree is the least n for which the nth differences are constant.
Count how many rows of differences it takes to reach a constant row.
The degree of a polynomial function can be found by examining the successive differences of the output values over equal-interval input values. The degree of the polynomial function is equal to the least value n for which the successive nth differences are constant.

records.text:
1.5.B · Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x); odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x).
Evaluate f(−x): equal to f(x) means even, equal to −f(x) means odd, otherwise neither.
An even function is graphically symmetric over the line x = 0 and analytically has the property f(−x) = f(x). An odd function is graphically symmetric about the point (0, 0) and analytically has the property f(−x) = −f(x). If n is even, p(x) = aₙxⁿ (with n ≥ 1 and aₙ ≠ 0) is an even function, and if n is odd, it is an odd function.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
Limit notation for end behavior and why the degree and the sign of the leading term determine the end behavior of a polynomial function.
As input values increase or decrease without bound, the leading term of a polynomial dominates all lower-degree terms. So the degree and the sign of the leading term determine the end behavior.
Zeros and extrema describe the middle of a polynomial's graph. End behavior describes the output values as the input values increase or decrease without bound, and the AP Exam expects it in limit notation.
records.excerpt: Limit notation for end behavior and why the degree and the sign of the leading term determine the end behavior of a polynomial function.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
records.heading: 1.6.A · End behavior is written with limit notation.
records.text:
1.6.A · End behavior is written with limit notation.
The input direction goes under lim, and the output behavior goes after the equals sign.
As the input values of a nonconstant polynomial function p increase without bound, the output values either increase without bound or decrease without bound. The corresponding notation is lim x→∞ p(x) = ∞ or lim x→∞ p(x) = −∞. As the input values decrease without bound, the output values also either increase or decrease without bound: lim x→−∞ p(x) = ∞ or lim x→−∞ p(x) = −∞.

1.6.A · The leading term dominates for input values of large magnitude.
A polynomial has the end behavior of its leading term.

records.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
records.text:
Rational Functions and End Behavior
Rational functions as quotients of polynomials, and how the quotient of the leading terms gives the end behavior, horizontal asymptotes, and slant asymptotes.
For input values of large magnitude, each polynomial is dominated by its leading term, so a rational function behaves like the quotient of the leading terms of its numerator and denominator.
Topic 1.6 found the end behavior of a polynomial from one leading term. A rational function has two polynomials, and its end behavior depends on which one dominates, or whether neither does.
records.excerpt: Rational functions as quotients of polynomials, and how the quotient of the leading terms gives the end behavior, horizontal asymptotes, and slant asymptotes.

records.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
records.heading: 1.7.A · A rational function is a quotient of two polynomial functions.
records.text:
1.7.A · A rational function is a quotient of two polynomial functions.
A rational function is p(x)/q(x), undefined wherever q(x) = 0.
A rational function is analytically represented as a quotient of two polynomial functions and gives a measure of the relative size of the polynomial function in the numerator compared to the polynomial function in the denominator for each value in the rational function’s domain. In symbols, r(x) = p(x)/q(x), and the domain excludes every real zero of q.

records.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
records.heading: 1.7.A · The end behavior comes from the quotient of the leading terms.
records.text:
1.7.A · The end behavior comes from the quotient of the leading terms.
Divide the leading terms. The result tells you which case you are in.
The end behavior of a rational function will be affected most by the polynomial with the greater degree, as its values will dominate the values of the rational function for input values of large magnitude. For input values of large magnitude, a polynomial is dominated by its leading term. Therefore, the end behavior of a rational function can be understood by examining the corresponding quotient of the leading terms.
Three cases for r(x) = p(x)/q(x)
Which polynomial dominates
Quotient of the leading terms
End behavior of r
The denominator (degree of q is greater)
A constant over a nonconstant polynomial
Horizontal asymptote y = 0
Neither (equal degrees)
A constant
Horizontal asymptote at that constant
The numerator (degree of p is greater)
A nonconstant polynomial
The end behavior of that polynomial; a slant asymptote if it is linear
For r(x) = (4x − 1)/(x² + 3), the quotient of the leading terms is 4x/x² = 4/x, so lim x→±∞ r(x) = 0. For r(x) = (3x² + 1)/(x² − 5), the quotient is 3x²/x² = 3, so the horizontal asymptote is y = 3.

records.heading: 1.7.A · A horizontal asymptote y = b means the output values get and stay arbitrarily close to b.
records.text:
1.7.A · A horizontal asymptote y = b means the output values get and stay arbitrarily close to b.
State a horizontal asymptote with limit notation for both directions when both apply.
When the graph of a rational function r has a horizontal asymptote at y = b, the output values get arbitrarily close to b and stay arbitrarily close to b as the input values increase or decrease without bound. The corresponding notation is lim x→∞ r(x) = b or lim x→−∞ r(x) = b.

Because the degrees of the numerator and denominator are equal, the quotient of the leading terms is 3x²/x² = 3. Therefore lim x→∞ r(x) = 3 and lim x→−∞ r(x) = 3, and the graph of r has a horizontal asymptote at y = 3.
An asymptote describes the ends of the graph only. The graph of r(x) = x/(x² + 1) has the horizontal asymptote y = 0, yet r(0) = 0, so the graph meets that line at the origin.

records.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
records.text:
Rational Functions and Zeros
The real zeros of a rational function, and how the real zeros of its numerator and denominator determine where it is positive or negative.
The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of its numerator that are in its domain. The real zeros of the numerator and of the denominator together mark the endpoints and asymptotes of the intervals where the function is positive or negative.
A quotient is 0 only when its numerator is 0 and the quotient is defined. That single fact gives the zeros of a rational function and is the starting point for solving rational inequalities.
records.excerpt: The real zeros of a rational function, and how the real zeros of its numerator and denominator determine where it is positive or negative.

records.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
records.heading: 1.8.A · The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of the numerator in its domain.
records.text:
1.8.A · The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of the numerator in its domain.
Find the real zeros of the numerator, then discard any that are not in the domain.
The real zeros of a rational function correspond to the real zeros of the numerator for such values in its domain. For r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 3)/(x − 1), the real zeros are x = 2 and x = −3. The value x = 1 makes the denominator 0, so 1 is not in the domain of r.
For r(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1), the numerator is 0 at x = 1 and x = −1, but x = 1 is not in the domain of r. The only real zero of r is x = −1. Topic 1.10 describes the graph at x = 1.

records.heading: 1.8.A · Real zeros are endpoints, and denominator zeros are asymptotes, for rational inequalities.
records.text:
1.8.A · Real zeros are endpoints, and denominator zeros are asymptotes, for rational inequalities.
Use the sign intervals, then decide each endpoint with the endpoint rules.
The real zeros of both polynomials of a rational function r are endpoints or asymptotes for the intervals satisfying r(x) ≥ 0 or r(x) ≤ 0. For r(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)/(x − 4), r(x) = 0 at x = −2 and x = 1, and r is undefined at x = 4. So r(x) ≥ 0 for −2 ≤ x ≤ 1 and for x > 4.
A real zero of the numerator in the domain satisfies r(x) ≥ 0 and r(x) ≤ 0, so include it.
For r(x) > 0 or r(x) < 0, exclude the real zeros of the numerator.
Always exclude a real zero of the denominator, because r is undefined there.
r(x) ≥ 0 for −2 ≤ x ≤ 1 and for x > 4. The value x = 4 is not included because r(4) is undefined.

records.title: Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
records.text:
Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
Where the graph of a rational function has a vertical asymptote, and how one-sided limits describe the output values near it.
Near a real zero of the denominator that is not cancelled by the numerator, the denominator's values are arbitrarily close to 0, so the output values of the rational function increase or decrease without bound.
Topic 1.8 left the real zeros of the denominator out of every solution. This topic studies the graph near those input values and the one-sided limit notation the AP Exam uses to describe it.
records.excerpt: Where the graph of a rational function has a vertical asymptote, and how one-sided limits describe the output values near it.

records.title: Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
records.heading: 1.9.A · A vertical asymptote occurs at a real zero of the denominator that is not a zero of the numerator.
records.text:
1.9.A · A vertical asymptote occurs at a real zero of the denominator that is not a zero of the numerator.
Compare the multiplicity of each real zero of the denominator with its multiplicity in the numerator.
If a is a real zero of the polynomial in the denominator of a rational function and is not also a real zero of the polynomial in the numerator, then the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = a. A vertical asymptote also occurs at x = a if the multiplicity of a as a real zero of the denominator is greater than its multiplicity as a real zero of the numerator.
For r(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 3), the denominator is 0 at x = 3 and the numerator is 4 there, so the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 3. For (x − 1)/(x − 1)², the value 1 has multiplicity 2 in the denominator and 1 in the numerator, so there is a vertical asymptote at x = 1 as well. The domain of each function leaves out the asymptote's x-value.

records.title: Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
records.heading: 1.9.A · One-sided limits describe the output values on each side of a vertical asymptote.
records.text:
1.9.A · One-sided limits describe the output values on each side of a vertical asymptote.
Find the sign of the numerator and the denominator just left and just right of the asymptote.
Near a vertical asymptote x = a, the values of the denominator are arbitrarily close to 0, so the values of r increase or decrease without bound. For input values near a and greater than a, write lim x→a⁺ r(x) = ∞ or lim x→a⁺ r(x) = −∞. For input values near a and less than a, write lim x→a⁻ r(x) = ∞ or lim x→a⁻ r(x) = −∞.
For r(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 3): just left of 3, the numerator is near 4 and the denominator is a small negative number, so lim x→3⁻ r(x) = −∞. Just right of 3, both are positive, so lim x→3⁺ r(x) = ∞.
lim x→3⁻ r(x) = −∞ and lim x→3⁺ r(x) = ∞, so the graph of r has a vertical asymptote at x = 3.

records.title: Rational Functions and Holes
records.text:
Rational Functions and Holes
When the graph of a rational function has a hole instead of a vertical asymptote, and how a limit locates the hole.
A rational function can be undefined at x = c without a vertical asymptote. If the multiplicity of c as a real zero of the numerator is at least its multiplicity in the denominator, the output values approach a single value L and the graph has a hole at (c, L).
Topic 1.9 compared multiplicities to find vertical asymptotes. This topic covers the other outcome of that comparison, and it uses a two-sided limit to give the coordinates of the hole.

records.title: Rational Functions and Holes
records.heading: 1.10.A · A hole occurs when the numerator's multiplicity is at least the denominator's.
records.text:
1.10.A · A hole occurs when the numerator's multiplicity is at least the denominator's.
Numerator multiplicity ≥ denominator multiplicity gives a hole. Otherwise there is a vertical asymptote.
If the multiplicity of a real zero in the numerator is greater than or equal to its multiplicity in the denominator, then the graph of the rational function has a hole at the corresponding input value. The function is undefined there, but after the common factors are removed, no factor of the denominator is 0 at that input value.

records.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
records.text:
Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
Factored and standard forms, polynomial long division, and the binomial theorem, and which form answers which question.
Equivalent analytic representations of the same function reveal different information. Factored form shows real zeros, holes, asymptotes, domain, and range. Standard form shows end behavior. Long division gives slant asymptotes, and the binomial theorem expands powers of binomials.
Earlier topics factored to find zeros, holes, and vertical asymptotes, and compared leading terms to find end behavior. This topic names those forms and adds two tools the CED requires: polynomial long division and the binomial theorem.

records.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
records.heading: 1.11.A · Factored form and standard form reveal different information.
records.text:
1.11.A · Factored form and standard form reveal different information.
Decide what you need to find, then rewrite in the form that shows it.
Because the factored form of a polynomial or rational function readily provides information about real zeros, it can reveal x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range. The standard form of a polynomial or rational function can reveal its end behavior. The information from different analytic representations of the same function can be used to answer questions in context.

records.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
records.heading: 1.11.B · Polynomial long division gives f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x).
records.text:
1.11.B · Polynomial long division gives f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x).
The quotient gives the slant asymptote, and the remainder term approaches 0 at the ends.
Polynomial long division is an algebraic process similar to numerical long division involving a quotient and remainder. If the polynomial f is divided by the polynomial g, then f can be rewritten as f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g. Dividing by g(x) gives f(x)/g(x) = q(x) + r(x)/g(x).
To divide x² + 3x + 5 by x − 1: x · (x − 1) = x² − x, leaving 4x + 5; then 4 · (x − 1) = 4x − 4, leaving a remainder of 9. So x² + 3x + 5 = (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9, and (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) = x + 4 + 9/(x − 1).
The result of polynomial long division is helpful in finding equations of slant asymptotes. As x increases or decreases without bound, 9/(x − 1) gets arbitrarily close to 0, so the slant asymptote is y = x + 4.
Show the identity that checks the division: (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9 = x² + 3x + 5.
Graph of (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) with its slant asymptote y = x + 4

records.heading: 1.11.C · The binomial theorem uses a row of Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)ⁿ.
records.text:
1.11.C · The binomial theorem uses a row of Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)ⁿ.
Use row n for the coefficients, and raise the whole of a and b, signs included, to their powers.
The binomial theorem uses the entries in a single row of Pascal's triangle to expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ, including polynomial functions of the form p(x) = (x + c)ⁿ, where c is a constant. Row n gives the coefficients, the powers of a decrease from n to 0, and the powers of b increase from 0 to n.

For (x + 2)⁴, row 4 is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, and the powers of 2 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. So (x + 2)⁴ = x⁴ + 8x³ + 24x² + 32x + 16. For (2x − 1)³, use a = 2x and b = −1: 8x³ − 12x² + 6x − 1.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.text:
Transformations of Functions
Additive and multiplicative transformations: translations, dilations, and reflections, combined transformations, and their effect on domain, range, and asymptotes.
Adding a constant to the input or output of a function translates its graph, and multiplying the input or output by a constant dilates it, possibly with a reflection. Changes to the input act horizontally, and changes to the output act vertically.
Each function type in AP Precalculus comes with a parent function. Transformations turn a parent function into a model that fits a context, which is why they appear in modeling questions throughout the course.
records.excerpt: Additive and multiplicative transformations: translations, dilations, and reflections, combined transformations, and their effect on domain, range, and asymptotes.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.heading: 1.12.A · Additive transformations translate the graph.
records.text:
1.12.A · Additive transformations translate the graph.
f(x + h) translates horizontally by −h units. f(x) + k translates vertically by k units.
The function g(x) = f(x) + k is an additive transformation of f that results in a vertical translation of the graph of f by k units. The function g(x) = f(x + h) is an additive transformation of f that results in a horizontal translation of the graph of f by −h units.
So f(x − 3) is a horizontal translation by 3 units (to the right), and f(x + 3) is a horizontal translation by −3 units (to the left). For g(x) = f(x − 3), g(5) = f(2), so the point (2, f(2)) of f appears at x = 5 on g.

records.text:
1.12.A · Multiplicative transformations dilate the graph and may reflect it.
a·f(x) dilates vertically by |a|. f(bx) dilates horizontally by 1/|b|. A negative a or b adds a reflection.
The function g(x) = a·f(x), where a ≠ 0, is a multiplicative transformation of f that results in a vertical dilation of the graph of f by a factor of |a|. If a < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the x-axis.
The function g(x) = f(bx), where b ≠ 0, is a multiplicative transformation of f that results in a horizontal dilation of the graph of f by a factor of 1/|b|. If b < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the y-axis.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.heading: 1.12.A · Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined.
records.text:
1.12.A · Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined.
Work from the inside out: find the input to f, then apply the dilation and translation of the output.
Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined, resulting in combinations of horizontal and vertical translations and dilations. The set of points before the transformations is the preimage, and the set of points after the transformations is the image.
Let f(x) = x² − 1, with zeros at x = −1 and x = 1, and let g(x) = 2f(x − 3). The graph of g is the graph of f translated horizontally by 3 units and dilated vertically by a factor of 2. The zeros move to x = 2 and x = 4, and the vertex (0, −1) moves to (3, −2).
When transformations are given in words, build the rule one step at a time. A horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, then a vertical dilation by a factor of 3, then a vertical translation by 5 units gives g(x) = 3f(x/2) + 5. To evaluate g(4), find f(4/2) = f(2) first.
g(x) = 3f(x/2) + 5, so g(4) = 3f(2) + 5. Show the input value given to f before applying the outside operations.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.heading: 1.12.A · A transformation can change the domain, the range, and the asymptotes.
records.text:
1.12.A · A transformation can change the domain, the range, and the asymptotes.
Transform the asymptotes, the domain, and the range along with the points.
The domain and range of a function that is a transformation of a parent function may be different from those of the parent function. Horizontal transformations move vertical asymptotes and change the domain. Vertical transformations move horizontal asymptotes and change the range.
The parent function f(x) = 1/x has the vertical asymptote x = 0 and the horizontal asymptote y = 0. For g(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, the asymptotes are x = 2 and y = 3, the domain is all real numbers x ≠ 2, and the range is all real numbers y ≠ 3. The parent function x² has range y ≥ 0, while h(x) = −2x² + 3 has range y ≤ 3.

records.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
records.text:
Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
Choosing a linear, quadratic, polynomial, or piecewise-defined model from a data set or context, and stating the assumptions and domain and range restrictions of a model.
A function model is chosen by matching how the quantities in a data set or context change to how a function type changes. Every model also carries assumptions about what stays consistent, and restrictions on its domain and range.
You now know how linear, quadratic, and other polynomial functions change. This topic asks which type to choose and how to justify the choice, a part that appears in free-response Question 1 and Question 2 of the AP Exam.
records.excerpt: Choosing a linear, quadratic, polynomial, or piecewise-defined model from a data set or context, and stating the assumptions and domain and range restrictions of a model.

records.heading: 1.13.A · The pattern of change in a data set or context points to a function type.
records.text:
1.13.A · The pattern of change in a data set or context points to a function type.
Describe how the output values change, then choose the function type that changes the same way.
Matching scenarios to function types
The data set or context shows
Function type
Roughly constant rates of change
Linear

Quadratic
A geometric context involving area or two dimensions
Quadratic
A geometric context involving volume or three dimensions
Cubic
Multiple real zeros, or multiple maxima or minima
Polynomial of higher degree
Roughly constant nonzero nth differences over equal-length input-value intervals
Polynomial of degree n
Different characteristics over different intervals
Piecewise-defined
An open box made by cutting squares of side x from the corners of a sheet has volume x(30 − 2x)(20 − 2x), a cubic function of x, because volume involves three dimensions. The area of a rectangle with a fixed perimeter is a quadratic function of its width, because area involves two dimensions.

1.13.A · A polynomial of degree n models roughly constant nonzero nth differences.
Name the constant difference, the level at which it appears, and the equal-length intervals.
A polynomial function of degree n models data sets or contextual scenarios that demonstrate roughly constant nonzero nth differences. Also, a polynomial function of degree n or less can be used to model a graph of n + 1 points with distinct input values, so 3 points can always be fit by a quadratic function or a line.

records.heading: 1.13.A · A piecewise-defined function models different behavior on different intervals.
records.text:
1.13.A · A piecewise-defined function models different behavior on different intervals.
Use a piecewise-defined model when the rate or pattern changes at a known input value.
A piecewise-defined function consists of a set of functions defined over nonoverlapping domain intervals. It is useful for modeling a data set or contextual scenario that demonstrates different characteristics over different intervals.
A parking garage charges $3 per hour for the first 2 hours and $1 per hour after that. The cost is modeled by C(t) = 3t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 and C(t) = 6 + (t − 2) for t > 2. Each piece is linear, but the rate of change is 3 dollars per hour on the first interval and 1 dollar per hour on the second.
Parking cost C(t): two linear pieces that meet at t = 2

records.heading: 1.13.B · Models have assumptions and domain and range restrictions.
records.text:
1.13.B · Models have assumptions and domain and range restrictions.
State the assumption, the domain, and the range in the language of the context.
A model may assume something is consistent, such as a constant growth rate or a fixed price.
A model may assume how the quantities change together, such as a constant rate of change for a linear model.
A model may require domain restrictions based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.
A model may require range restrictions, such as rounding to whole numbers, based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.
A ball thrown from a height of 5 feet has height h(t) = −16t² + 48t + 5 feet after t seconds. The model assumes only gravity acts on the ball. Its domain is restricted to 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.101, from the throw until the ball lands, and its range to 0 ≤ h(t) ≤ 41, since the maximum height is h(1.5) = 41.

records.title: Function Model Construction and Application
records.text:
Function Model Construction and Application
Constructing polynomial, piecewise-defined, and rational models from conditions, transformations, or regression, and applying a model to answer questions with units.
A model is constructed from restrictions in a context, from transformations of a parent function, or from a regression on data. Once constructed, its values, rates of change, average rates of change, and asymptotes answer questions about the context, with units.
Topic 1.13 chose the function type. This topic finds the specific function and uses it. Free-response Question 2 on the AP Exam follows this path: build the model, compute an average rate of change with units, then interpret and restrict the model.

records.text:
1.14.A · A model can be constructed from restrictions in a context.
Write one equation per condition, then solve for the constants.
A model can be constructed based on restrictions identified in a mathematical or contextual scenario. If a cubic has real zeros at −2, 1, and 3 and passes through (0, 12), then p(x) = a(x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3). At x = 0 this gives 6a = 12, so a = 2 and p(x) = 2(x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3).

records.text:
1.14.A · A model can be constructed with transformations of a parent function.
Translations place the vertex or asymptotes; one more point fixes the dilation.
A model of a data set or a contextual scenario can be constructed using transformations of the parent function. Choose the parent function with the right shape, then use the features of the context to choose the translations and dilations.
A quadratic model with vertex (2, 5) through (0, 1) has the form a(x − 2)² + 5. Then 1 = 4a + 5, so a = −1. A rational model with a vertical asymptote at x = 1 and a horizontal asymptote at y = 2 through (3, 3) has the form a/(x − 1) + 2. Then 3 = a/2 + 2, so a = 2.

records.title: Function Model Construction and Application
records.heading: 1.14.B · Inversely proportional quantities are modeled by rational functions.
records.text:
1.14.B · Inversely proportional quantities are modeled by rational functions.
Inverse proportionality gives a rational model k/x or k/x². Asymptotes describe long-run values.
Data sets and contextual scenarios involving quantities that are inversely proportional can often be modeled by rational functions. For example, the magnitudes of the gravitational force and the electromagnetic force between objects are inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and so is the intensity of light from a point source.
If the intensity of light is 50 lux at 2 meters from a source and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance d, then I(d) = k/d² with 50 = k/4, so k = 200 and I(d) = 200/d². At d = 5 meters the model predicts I(5) = 8 lux.

records.heading: 1.14.C · A model is applied to answer questions, with appropriate units.
records.text:
1.14.C · A model is applied to answer questions, with appropriate units.
Every answer in context names the quantity, the units, and the interval or input value.
A model can be used to draw conclusions about the data set or context, including answering key questions and predicting values, rates of change, average rates of change, and changing rates of change. Appropriate units of measure should be extracted or inferred from the context.
For I(d) = 200/d², the average rate of change from d = 2 to d = 5 is (I(5) − I(2))/(5 − 2) = (8 − 50)/3 = −14 lux per meter. For a store's revenue R(p) = p(80 − 4p), in dollars, at price p dollars, the zeros p = 0 and p = 20 mean no revenue, and the maximum is R(10) = 400 dollars at a price of $10.
From d = 2 meters to d = 5 meters, on average, the intensity of the light decreased at a rate of 14 lux per meter.

records.title: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences
records.text:
Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences
Sequences as functions of the whole numbers, arithmetic sequences with a common difference, geometric sequences with a common ratio, and the general term of each.
An arithmetic sequence changes by adding the same amount each step. A geometric sequence changes by multiplying by the same amount each step. Unit 2 builds linear and exponential functions from these two kinds of change.
Unit 1 compared average rates of change over equal-length intervals. Sequences are the simplest place to see the two patterns Unit 2 is about: constant change and proportional change.
records.excerpt: Sequences as functions of the whole numbers, arithmetic sequences with a common difference, geometric sequences with a common ratio, and the general term of each.

records.title: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences
records.heading: 2.1.A · A sequence is a function from the whole numbers to the real numbers.
records.text:
2.1.A · A sequence is a function from the whole numbers to the real numbers.
A sequence takes whole-number inputs, so its graph is a set of separate points.
A sequence is a function from the whole numbers to the real numbers. Consequently, the graph of a sequence consists of discrete points instead of a curve.
The input is the position n = 0, 1, 2, …, and the output is the term aₙ. Writing a₃ = 14 means the function value at n = 3 is 14, the same idea as f(3) = 14.
The arithmetic sequence aₙ = 5 + 3n for n = 0 to 5: separate points, not a curve

2.1.A · An arithmetic sequence has a common difference.
Arithmetic: aₙ = a₀ + dn, or aₙ = aₖ + d(n − k) from any known term.
Successive terms in an arithmetic sequence have a common difference, or constant rate of change.

records.title: Change in Linear and Exponential Functions
records.text:
Change in Linear and Exponential Functions
Linear functions as the real-number version of arithmetic sequences, exponential functions as the real-number version of geometric sequences, and how to tell additive change from multiplicative change.
Linear functions are built on repeated addition of a constant rate of change. Exponential functions are built on repeated multiplication by a constant ratio. Two values are enough to determine either one.
Topic 2.1 wrote arithmetic and geometric sequences on the whole numbers. This topic extends them to functions of all real numbers and gives the test the AP Exam uses to choose between a linear and an exponential model.
records.excerpt: Linear functions as the real-number version of arithmetic sequences, exponential functions as the real-number version of geometric sequences, and how to tell additive change from multiplicative change.

records.title: Change in Linear and Exponential Functions
records.heading: 2.2.A · Linear functions are comparable to arithmetic sequences.
records.text:
2.2.A · Linear functions are comparable to arithmetic sequences.
f(x) = b + mx and f(x) = yᵢ + m(x − xᵢ) match aₙ = a₀ + dn and aₙ = aₖ + d(n − k).
Linear functions of the form f(x) = b + mx are similar to arithmetic sequences of the form aₙ = a₀ + dn, as both can be expressed as an initial value (b or a₀) plus repeated addition of a constant rate of change, the slope (m or d).
Similar to arithmetic sequences of the form aₙ = aₖ + d(n − k), which are based on a known difference, d, and a kth term, linear functions can be expressed in the form f(x) = yᵢ + m(x − xᵢ) based on a known slope, m, and a point, (xᵢ, yᵢ).
Example: a line with slope −2 through (4, 9) is f(x) = 9 − 2(x − 4). Expanding gives f(x) = 17 − 2x, so the initial value is f(0) = 17.

f(x) = abˣ and f(x) = yᵢb^(x − xᵢ) match gₙ = g₀rⁿ and gₙ = gₖr^(n − k).
Exponential functions of the form f(x) = abˣ are similar to geometric sequences of the form gₙ = g₀rⁿ, as both can be expressed as an initial value (a or g₀) times repeated multiplication by a constant ratio (b or r).
Similar to geometric sequences of the form gₙ = gₖr^(n − k), which are based on a known ratio, r, and a kth term, exponential functions can be expressed in the form f(x) = yᵢb^(x − xᵢ) based on a known ratio, b, and a point, (xᵢ, yᵢ).

Equal differences mean linear. Equal ratios (not 0 or 1) mean exponential.

records.title: Exponential Functions
records.text:
Exponential Functions
The general form f(x) = abˣ, its initial value and base, exponential growth and decay, why exponential functions have no extrema or points of inflection, and their end behavior.
Every key characteristic of an exponential function in general form follows from two numbers: the initial value a and the base b. Their signs and sizes decide whether the function grows or decays, its concavity, and its end behavior.
Topic 2.2 introduced f(x) = abˣ as the real-number version of a geometric sequence. This topic names its parts and the behavior the AP Exam expects you to read from them.
records.excerpt: The general form f(x) = abˣ, its initial value and base, exponential growth and decay, why exponential functions have no extrema or points of inflection, and their end behavior.

records.title: Exponential Functions
records.heading: 2.3.A · The general form of an exponential function is f(x) = abˣ.
records.text:
2.3.A · The general form of an exponential function is f(x) = abˣ.
a is the initial value, b is the base; a > 0 with b > 1 is growth, and a > 0 with 0 < b < 1 is decay.
The general form of an exponential function is f(x) = abˣ, with the initial value a, where a ≠ 0, and the base b, where b > 0, and b ≠ 1. When a > 0 and b > 1, the exponential function is said to demonstrate exponential growth. When a > 0 and 0 < b < 1, the exponential function is said to demonstrate exponential decay.
When the natural numbers are input values in an exponential function, the input value specifies the number of factors of the base to be applied to the function's initial value. The domain of an exponential function is all real numbers.
Example: for f(x) = 5(0.8)ˣ, the initial value is f(0) = 5 and the base is 0.8. f(2) = 5(0.8)(0.8) = 3.2 applies two factors of 0.8. Because a > 0 and 0 < b < 1, f demonstrates exponential decay.

records.title: Exponential Functions
records.heading: 2.3.A · Exponential functions are always increasing or always decreasing.
records.text:
2.3.A · Exponential functions are always increasing or always decreasing.
No turning points and no inflection points: one direction, one concavity.
Because the output values of exponential functions in general form are proportional over equal-length input-value intervals, exponential functions are always increasing or always decreasing, and their graphs are always concave up or always concave down. Consequently, exponential functions do not have extrema except on a closed interval, and their graphs do not have points of inflection.

If the output values of the function f are not proportional over equal-length input-value intervals, but the output values of an additive transformation of f are proportional over equal-length input-value intervals, then f can be modeled by an additive transformation of an exponential function.
Example: the values 4, 5, 7, 11 are not proportional. Subtracting 3 gives 1, 2, 4, 8, which are proportional with ratio 2. So the data can be modeled by y = 2ˣ + 3.
f has no relative maximum because an exponential function in general form is always increasing or always decreasing.

records.title: Exponential Functions
records.heading: 2.3.A · End behavior: unbounded on one side, approaching zero on the other.
records.text:
2.3.A · End behavior: unbounded on one side, approaching zero on the other.
One end goes to ±∞; the other gets arbitrarily close to 0.
For an exponential function in general form, as the input values increase or decrease without bound, the output values will increase or decrease without bound or will get arbitrarily close to zero. That is, for an exponential function in general form, lim x→±∞ abˣ = ∞, lim x→±∞ abˣ = −∞, or lim x→±∞ abˣ = 0.
Exponential growth g(x) = 2(1.5)ˣ and exponential decay h(x) = 2(0.5)ˣ, both with initial value 2
For g(x) = 2(1.5)ˣ, lim x→∞ g(x) = ∞ and lim x→−∞ g(x) = 0. For h(x) = 2(0.5)ˣ, lim x→∞ h(x) = 0 and lim x→−∞ h(x) = ∞. In each case the line y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote on one side.

records.title: Exponential Function Manipulation
records.text:
Exponential Function Manipulation
The product, power, and negative exponent properties, unit-fraction exponents as roots, and how horizontal translations and dilations of exponential functions become vertical dilations and changes of base.
The properties of exponents are not just rules for simplifying. They show that shifting an exponential graph sideways is the same as stretching it vertically, and squeezing it sideways is the same as changing its base.
Topic 2.3 described f(x) = abˣ. Free-response Question 4 on the AP Exam asks you to rewrite exponential expressions in equivalent forms without a calculator, using exactly these properties.
records.excerpt: The product, power, and negative exponent properties, unit-fraction exponents as roots, and how horizontal translations and dilations of exponential functions become vertical dilations and changes of base.

records.title: Exponential Function Manipulation
records.heading: 2.4.A · The product property: a horizontal translation is a vertical dilation.
records.text:
2.4.A · The product property: a horizontal translation is a vertical dilation.
b^(x + k) = bᵏ·bˣ: shift left by k, or stretch by bᵏ. Same graph.
The product property for exponents states that bᵐbⁿ = b^(m + n). Graphically, this property implies that every horizontal translation of an exponential function, f(x) = b^(x + k), is equivalent to a vertical dilation, f(x) = b^(x + k) = bˣbᵏ = abˣ, where a = bᵏ.
Example: 2^(x + 3) = 2ˣ·2³ = 8(2)ˣ. Translating the graph of y = 2ˣ horizontally by −3 units gives the same graph as dilating it vertically by a factor of 8.
y = 2^(x + 3) and y = 8(2)ˣ are the same function
5^(x − 2) = 5ˣ·5⁻² = (1/25)·5ˣ. Show the product property step before writing the coefficient.
records.excerpt: b^(x + k) = bᵏ·bˣ: shift left by k, or stretch by bᵏ. Same graph.

records.title: Exponential Function Manipulation
records.heading: 2.4.A · The power property: a horizontal dilation is a change of base.
records.text:
2.4.A · The power property: a horizontal dilation is a change of base.
b^(cx) = (b^c)ˣ: a horizontal dilation changes the base to b^c.
The power property for exponents states that (bᵐ)ⁿ = b^(mn). Graphically, this property implies that every horizontal dilation of an exponential function, f(x) = b^(cx), is equivalent to a change of the base of an exponential function, f(x) = (b^c)ˣ, where b^c is a constant and c ≠ 0.
Example: 3^(2x) = (3²)ˣ = 9ˣ, and 16^(x/4) = (16^(1/4))ˣ = 2ˣ. A horizontal dilation by a factor of 1/2 turns base 3 into base 9.
4^(3x + 1) = 4^(3x)·4¹ = 4(4³)ˣ = 4(64)ˣ. Use the product property first, then the power property.

records.title: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
records.text:
Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
Recognizing proportional growth in data, building an exponential model from a ratio and initial value or from two points, the natural base e, growth factors and percent change, and using equivalent forms to answer questions in context.
When a quantity changes by the same factor over each equal-length interval, an exponential model fits. Its base is that factor, and rewriting the model in an equivalent form can answer a different question about the same situation.
Free-response Question 2 on the AP Exam often gives two data points from a context and asks you to build an exponential model by solving a system of equations, then interpret the model and its limitations.
records.excerpt: Recognizing proportional growth in data, building an exponential model from a ratio and initial value or from two points, the natural base e, growth factors and percent change, and using equivalent forms to answer questions in context.

records.title: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 2.5.A · Exponential functions model proportional growth patterns.
records.text:
2.5.A · Exponential functions model proportional growth patterns.
Look for a constant ratio, after subtracting a constant if needed.
Exponential functions model growth patterns where successive output values over equal-length input-value intervals are proportional. When the input values are whole numbers, exponential functions model situations of repeated multiplication of a constant to an initial value.
A constant may need to be added to the dependent variable values of a data set to reveal a proportional growth pattern.

records.title: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 2.5.A · Build an exponential model from a ratio and initial value, or from two points.
records.text:
2.5.A · Build an exponential model from a ratio and initial value, or from two points.
Two input-output pairs give two equations; divide them to eliminate a.
An exponential function model can be constructed from an appropriate ratio and initial value or from two input-output pairs. The initial value and the base can be found by solving a system of equations resulting from the two input-output pairs.
Example: a population is 500 when t = 2 years and 720 when t = 4 years. Using P(t) = abᵗ, the system is ab² = 500 and ab⁴ = 720. Dividing gives b² = 1.44, so b = 1.2, and then a = 500/1.44 ≈ 347.222. The model is P(t) ≈ 347.222(1.2)ᵗ.
Exponential function models can be constructed by applying transformations to f(x) = abˣ based on characteristics of a contextual scenario or data set. Exponential function models can be constructed for a data set with technology using exponential regressions.
The natural base e, which is approximately 2.718, is often used as the base in exponential functions that model contextual scenarios.
Using the given data, ab² = 500 and ab⁴ = 720. Then (ab⁴)/(ab²) = b² = 720/500 = 1.44, so b = 1.2 and a = 500/1.2² ≈ 347.222.

records.title: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 2.5.B · Growth factors, percent change, and equivalent forms.
records.text:
2.5.B · Growth factors, percent change, and equivalent forms.
b = 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay; rewrite the exponent to change the time unit.
For an exponential model in general form f(x) = abˣ, the base of the exponent, b, can be understood as a growth factor in successive unit changes in the input values and is related to a percent change in context.
A savings balance modeled by B(t) = 1200(1.03)ᵗ, with t in years, has growth factor 1.03: it increases by 3% per year. A value modeled by V(t) = 18000(0.85)ᵗ has growth factor 0.85: it decreases by 15% per year.
Equivalent forms of an exponential function can reveal different properties of the function. For example, if d represents number of days, then the base of f(d) = 2ᵈ indicates that the quantity increases by a factor of 2 every day, but the equivalent form f(d) = (2⁷)^(d/7) indicates that the quantity increases by a factor of 2⁷ every week.
Exponential models can be used to predict values for the dependent variable, depending on the contextual constraints on the domain, and may be used to determine values of the independent variable.
B(10) = 1200(1.03)¹⁰ ≈ 1612.700. According to the model, the balance after 10 years is about $1612.70. The balance reaches $2400 when 1200(1.03)ᵗ = 2400, at t ≈ 23.450 years.

records.title: Competing Function Model Validation
records.text:
Competing Function Model Validation
Comparing linear, quadratic, and exponential models for the same data, residuals and residual plots, judging whether a model is appropriate, and how errors show where a model underestimates or overestimates.
Several models can fit the same data reasonably well. Residuals, the leftover differences between the data and a model, show which model captures the pattern: an appropriate model leaves residuals with no pattern.
Topics 1.14 and 2.5 built models with regressions. This topic decides between competing models, which is a reasoning skill the AP Exam asks you to justify with residuals or context.
records.excerpt: Comparing linear, quadratic, and exponential models for the same data, residuals and residual plots, judging whether a model is appropriate, and how errors show where a model underestimates or overestimates.

records.title: Competing Function Model Validation
records.heading: 2.6.A · Several function types can model the same data.
records.text:
2.6.A · Several function types can model the same data.
More than one model can fit; context and residuals decide which is most appropriate.
Two variables in a data set that demonstrate a slightly changing rate of change can be modeled by linear, quadratic, and exponential function models.
Models can be compared based on contextual clues and applicability to determine which model is most appropriate.

Linear regression gives y ≈ 1.205 + 1.691x, and exponential regression gives y ≈ 2.034(1.392)ˣ. Both follow the general upward trend, so the graphs alone do not settle which model is more appropriate.
Contextual clues matter too. If y is the number of users of an app that spreads by sharing, growth that compounds suggests an exponential model. If y can never exceed a fixed limit, a model that increases without bound is not appropriate far from the data.

records.heading: 2.6.B · A model is appropriate if its residual plot appears without pattern.
records.text:
2.6.B · A model is appropriate if its residual plot appears without pattern.
Residual = actual − predicted. Pattern means the model misses something; no pattern means appropriate.
For a given value of an independent variable, a residual of a regression is the actual value of the dependent variable minus the value predicted by the function regression model.
A residual plot is a graphical representation of the residuals of a regression, with the residuals on the vertical axis and the independent variable on the horizontal axis. A model is justified as appropriate for a data set if the residual plot appears without pattern.
Residual plot for the linear model: a curved pattern
Residual plot for the exponential model: no pattern
The exponential model is more appropriate because its residual plot appears without pattern, while the residuals of the linear model are positive, then negative, then positive.

records.title: Competing Function Model Validation
records.heading: 2.6.B · Errors show where a model underestimates or overestimates.
records.text:
2.6.B · Errors show where a model underestimates or overestimates.
Positive residual: model underestimates. Negative residual: model overestimates.
For given values of an independent variable, the errors in a model can relate to the signed differences in the values of the dependent variable predicted by the function regression model and the actual values OR the unsigned absolute values of the residuals. Errors may reveal that the model underestimates or overestimates actual values on a given input-value interval. The data set and context can provide clues as to whether underestimates or overestimates are preferred on a given input-value interval.
A positive residual means the actual value is greater than the predicted value, so the model underestimates there. A negative residual means the model overestimates. In the linear model above, the residuals are negative for 1 ≤ x ≤ 4, so the linear model overestimates on that interval.
Context decides which kind of error is worse. A model for how much medicine remains in the body might prefer to overestimate on an interval, so a second dose is not given too early, while a model for how many seats a venue holds might prefer to underestimate.

records.title: Composition of Functions
records.text:
Composition of Functions
Evaluating f ∘ g from tables, graphs, and formulas, why composition is not commutative, the identity function, building f(g(x)) analytically, and decomposing a function into simpler functions.
In a composition, the output of one function becomes the input of the next. Reading from the inside out evaluates it, substituting builds it, and looking for the inner and outer steps takes it apart.
Free-response Question 1 on the AP Exam regularly asks for values of a composite function from a table or a graph. Composition is also the language of inverse functions in Topic 2.8.
records.excerpt: Evaluating f ∘ g from tables, graphs, and formulas, why composition is not commutative, the identity function, building f(g(x)) analytically, and decomposing a function into simpler functions.

records.title: Composition of Functions
records.heading: 2.7.A · The outputs of g become the inputs of f.
records.text:
2.7.A · The outputs of g become the inputs of f.
Inside first: find g(x), then use it as the input of f.
If f and g are functions, the composite function f ∘ g maps a set of input values to a set of output values such that the output values of g are used as input values of f. For this reason, the domain of the composite function is restricted to those input values of g for which the corresponding output value is in the domain of f. (f ∘ g)(x) can also be represented as f(g(x)).
Values for the composite function f ∘ g can be calculated or estimated from the graphical, numerical, analytical, or verbal representations of f and g by using output values from g as input values for f.

records.title: Composition of Functions
records.heading: 2.7.A · Composition is not commutative; the identity function changes nothing.
records.text:
2.7.A · Composition is not commutative; the identity function changes nothing.
f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) usually differ; composing with x leaves a function unchanged.
The composition of functions is not commutative; that is, f ∘ g and g ∘ f are typically different functions; therefore, f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are typically different values.
Example: with f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, f(g(3)) = f(7) = 49 but g(f(3)) = g(9) = 19.
If the function f(x) = x is composed with any function g, the resulting composite function is the same as g; that is, g(f(x)) = f(g(x)) = g(x). The function f(x) = x is called the identity function. When composing two functions, the identity function acts in the same way as 0, the additive identity, when adding two numbers and 1, the multiplicative identity, when multiplying two numbers.

records.heading: 2.7.B · Build f(g(x)) by substituting g(x) for every x in f.
records.text:
2.7.B · Build f(g(x)) by substituting g(x) for every x in f.
Replace every x in the outer function with the whole inner function, in parentheses.
Function composition is useful for relating two quantities that are not directly related by an existing formula.
When analytic representations of the functions f and g are available, an analytic representation of f(g(x)) can be constructed by substituting g(x) for every instance of x in f.
A numerical or graphical representation of f ∘ g can often be constructed by calculating or estimating values for (x, f(g(x))).
Example: the radius of a ripple is r(t) = 3t centimeters after t seconds, and the area of a circle of radius r is A(r) = πr². Area and time are not related by a given formula, but the composition A(r(t)) = π(3t)² = 9πt² relates them.
If f(x) = √(x + 4) and g(x) = x² − 3, then f(g(x)) = √((x² − 3) + 4) = √(x² + 1).

records.title: Inverse Functions
records.text:
Inverse Functions
When a function is invertible, how an inverse reverses input-output pairs, composition with the identity function, domains and ranges of inverses, reflecting a graph over y = x, and finding an inverse analytically.
An inverse function runs a function backward: it sends each output back to the one input that produced it. That only works when no output comes from two different inputs, which sometimes requires restricting the domain.
Topic 2.7 introduced composition and the identity function. Inverses are defined by composition, and Topic 2.10 uses them to build logarithmic functions as inverses of exponential functions.
records.excerpt: When a function is invertible, how an inverse reverses input-output pairs, composition with the identity function, domains and ranges of inverses, reflecting a graph over y = x, and finding an inverse analytically.

records.title: Inverse Functions
records.heading: 2.8.A · A function is invertible if each output comes from a unique input.
records.text:
2.8.A · A function is invertible if each output comes from a unique input.
Invertible means no output is shared; the inverse swaps every (a, b) to (b, a).
On a specified domain, a function, f, has an inverse function, or is invertible, if each output value of f is mapped from a unique input value. The domain of a function may be restricted in many ways to make the function invertible.
An inverse function can be thought of as a reverse mapping of the function. An inverse function, f⁻¹, maps the output values of a function, f, on its invertible domain to their corresponding input values; that is, if f(a) = b, then f⁻¹(b) = a. Alternately, on its invertible domain, if a function consists of input-output pairs (a, b), then the inverse function consists of input-output pairs (b, a).
Example: f(x) = x² is not invertible on all real numbers, because f(−3) = f(3) = 9. Restricted to x ≥ 0, each output comes from one input, and f⁻¹(x) = √x.
records.excerpt: Invertible means no output is shared; the inverse swaps every (a, b) to (b, a).

f(f⁻¹(x)) = f⁻¹(f(x)) = x, and the domain and range trade places.

records.title: Inverse Functions
records.heading: 2.8.B · Find an inverse by reflecting the graph or reversing the operations.
records.text:
2.8.B · Find an inverse by reflecting the graph or reversing the operations.
Swap x and y, then solve for y. The graph reflects over y = x.
The inverse of the graph of the function y = f(x) can be found by reversing the roles of the x- and y-axes; that is, by reflecting the graph of the function over the graph of the identity function h(x) = x.
f(x) = 3x + 5 and its inverse f⁻¹(x) = (x − 5)/3, reflections of each other over y = x
The inverse of the function can be found by determining the inverse operations to reverse the mapping. One method for finding the inverse of the function f is reversing the roles of x and y in the equation y = f(x), then solving for y = f⁻¹(x).
y = 3x + 5. Reverse the roles of x and y: x = 3y + 5. Solve: y = (x − 5)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 5)/3.
In addition to limiting the domain of a function to obtain an inverse function, contextual restrictions may also limit the applicability of an inverse function.

records.title: Logarithmic Expressions
records.text:
Logarithmic Expressions
What log_b c means, evaluating logarithms with and without technology, the common logarithm, and logarithmic scales.
A logarithm answers one question: what exponent turns the base into this number? Every logarithm statement is an exponential statement read the other way.
Topics 2.3 to 2.5 asked for outputs of exponential functions. Logarithms ask for the input instead, which is the step needed to solve exponential equations and to build logarithmic functions in Topic 2.10.
records.excerpt: What log_b c means, evaluating logarithms with and without technology, the common logarithm, and logarithmic scales.

records.title: Logarithmic Expressions
records.heading: 2.9.A · log_b c is the exponent that b must be raised to in order to obtain c.
records.text:
2.9.A · log_b c is the exponent that b must be raised to in order to obtain c.
log_b c = a means bᵃ = c. No base written means base 10.
The logarithmic expression log_b c is equal to, or represents, the value that the base b must be exponentially raised to in order to obtain the value c. That is, log_b c = a if and only if bᵃ = c, where a and c are constants, b > 0, and b ≠ 1. (when the base of a logarithmic expression is not specified, it is understood as the common logarithm with a base of 10)
Each logarithm statement is an exponential statement

Exponential form

2⁵ = 32
2 must be raised to 5 to obtain 32.
log₃ (1/27) = −3
3⁻³ = 1/27
3 must be raised to −3 to obtain 1/27.
log 0.01 = −2
10⁻² = 0.01
The common logarithm has base 10.
log₉ 3 = 1/2
9^(1/2) = 3
A unit-fraction exponent is a root.

records.title: Logarithmic Expressions
records.heading: 2.9.A · Some logarithms are exact; others are estimated with technology.
records.text:
2.9.A · Some logarithms are exact; others are estimated with technology.
Rewrite as powers of a common base for exact values; estimate the rest with technology.
The values of some logarithmic expressions are readily accessible through basic arithmetic while other values can be estimated through the use of technology.
log₅ 125 = 3 is exact, because 125 = 5³. log 40 is not an integer: since 10¹ = 10 and 10² = 100, log 40 is between 1 and 2, and technology gives log 40 ≈ 1.602.
When the argument can be written as a power of a common base, rewrite both: log₈ 4 asks for a with 8ᵃ = 4. Since 8 = 2³ and 4 = 2², (2³)ᵃ = 2², so 3a = 2 and log₈ 4 = 2/3.
On the no-calculator Question 4, find exact values such as log₂ 8 = 3. Use a decimal only when a calculator is allowed and the value is not exact.
