records.heading: 2.9.A · On a logarithmic scale, each unit is a multiplicative change.
records.text:
2.9.A · On a logarithmic scale, each unit is a multiplicative change.
Equal steps on a log scale mean equal factors, not equal differences.
On a logarithmic scale, each unit represents a multiplicative change of the base of the logarithm. For example, on a standard scale, the units might be 0, 1, 2, …, while on a logarithmic scale, using logarithm base 10, the units might be 10⁰, 10¹, 10², ….

Moving one unit to the right multiplies the value by 10, so values that differ by many orders of magnitude, such as the intensity of a whisper and a jet engine, fit on one scale.

records.title: Inverses of Exponential Functions
records.text:
Inverses of Exponential Functions
The general form of a logarithmic function, how logarithmic growth reverses exponential growth, log_b x and bˣ as inverse functions, and reflecting graphs and ordered pairs over y = x.
The exponential function bˣ and the logarithmic function log_b x undo each other. Every fact about one becomes a fact about the other with inputs and outputs switched.
Topic 2.8 found inverses by reversing input-output pairs, and Topic 2.9 defined log_b c. Here the two meet: log_b x is the inverse function of bˣ.

records.heading: 2.10.A · The general form of a logarithmic function is f(x) = a log_b x.
records.text:
2.10.A · The general form of a logarithmic function is f(x) = a log_b x.
f(x) = a log_b x with b > 0, b ≠ 1, and a ≠ 0.
The general form of a logarithmic function is f(x) = a log_b x, with base b, where b > 0, b ≠ 1, and a ≠ 0.
Example: f(x) = 3 log₂ x has a = 3 and base 2. Then f(8) = 3 log₂ 8 = 3(3) = 9.

records.title: Inverses of Exponential Functions
records.heading: 2.10.A · Exponential growth and logarithmic growth trade the roles of addition and multiplication.
records.text:
2.10.A · Exponential growth and logarithmic growth trade the roles of addition and multiplication.
Exponential: add to inputs, multiply outputs. Logarithmic: multiply inputs, add to outputs.
The way in which input and output values vary together have an inverse relationship in exponential and logarithmic functions. Output values of general-form exponential functions change proportionally as input values increase in equal-length intervals. However, input values of general-form logarithmic functions change proportionally as output values increase in equal-length intervals. Alternately, exponential growth is characterized by output values changing multiplicatively as input values change additively, whereas logarithmic growth is characterized by output values changing additively as input values change multiplicatively.

records.heading: 2.10.A · log_b x and bˣ are inverse functions.
records.text:
2.10.A · log_b x and bˣ are inverse functions.
Switch every ordered pair of bˣ to get log_b x; the graphs reflect over y = x.
f(x) = log_b x and g(x) = bˣ, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1, are inverse functions. That is, g(f(x)) = f(g(x)) = x.
The graph of the logarithmic function f(x) = log_b x, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1, is a reflection of the graph of the exponential function g(x) = bˣ, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1, over the graph of the identity function h(x) = x.
g(x) = 2ˣ and f(x) = log₂ x, reflections of each other over the line y = x
If (s, t) is an ordered pair of the exponential function g(x) = bˣ, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1, then (t, s) is an ordered pair of the logarithmic function f(x) = log_b x, where b > 0 and b ≠ 1.
Because (3, 125) is on the graph of y = 5ˣ, the point (125, 3) is on the graph of y = log₅ x, so log₅ 125 = 3.

records.title: Logarithmic Functions
records.text:
Logarithmic Functions
The domain, range, vertical asymptote, and end behavior of logarithmic functions, why they have no extrema or points of inflection, and recognizing a logarithmic pattern after an additive transformation.
A logarithmic function is an exponential function reflected over y = x, so every characteristic of bˣ appears in log_b x with the roles of x and y switched: a horizontal asymptote becomes a vertical one, and an all-real domain becomes an all-real range.
Topic 2.3 listed the key characteristics of exponential functions. This topic lists the matching characteristics of logarithmic functions, which the AP Exam uses in both multiple-choice and free-response questions.
records.excerpt: The domain, range, vertical asymptote, and end behavior of logarithmic functions, why they have no extrema or points of inflection, and recognizing a logarithmic pattern after an additive transformation.

records.title: Logarithmic Functions
records.heading: 2.11.A · Domain x > 0, range all real numbers, and a vertical asymptote at x = 0.
records.text:
2.11.A · Domain x > 0, range all real numbers, and a vertical asymptote at x = 0.
Domain x > 0, range all reals, vertical asymptote x = 0, unbounded at both ends.
The domain of a logarithmic function in general form is any real number greater than zero, and its range is all real numbers.
With their limited domain, logarithmic functions in general form are vertically asymptotic to x = 0, with an end behavior that is unbounded. That is, for a logarithmic function in general form, lim x→0⁺ a log_b x = ±∞ and lim x→∞ a log_b x = ±∞.
f(x) = log₂ x and g(x) = −2 log₃ x, both with the vertical asymptote x = 0
For f(x) = log₂ x, lim x→0⁺ f(x) = −∞ and lim x→∞ f(x) = ∞. The graph of f has a vertical asymptote at x = 0.

records.heading: 2.11.A · Logarithmic functions are always increasing or always decreasing.
records.text:
2.11.A · Logarithmic functions are always increasing or always decreasing.
One direction and one concavity everywhere: no extrema, no inflection points.
Because logarithmic functions are inverses of exponential functions, logarithmic functions are also always increasing or always decreasing, and their graphs are either always concave up or always concave down. Consequently, logarithmic functions do not have extrema except on a closed interval, and their graphs do not have points of inflection.

records.heading: 2.11.A · Recognizing a logarithmic pattern after an additive transformation.
records.text:
2.11.A · Recognizing a logarithmic pattern after an additive transformation.
If shifting the inputs makes them proportional over equal output steps, the function is logarithmic.
The additive transformation function g(x) = f(x + k), where k ≠ 0, of a logarithmic function f in general form does not have input values that are proportional over equal-length output-value intervals. However, if the input values of the additive transformation function, g(x) = f(x + k), of any function f are proportional over equal-length output value intervals, then f is logarithmic.

The inputs 0, 1, 3, 7 are not proportional, but the outputs increase by 1 each time. Adding 1 to each input gives 1, 2, 4, 8, which are proportional with ratio 2. So g(x) = f(x + 1) with f logarithmic, and g(x) = log₂ (x + 1) fits the table.

records.title: Logarithmic Function Manipulation
records.text:
Logarithmic Function Manipulation
The product, power, and change of base properties for logarithms, the natural logarithm, and how horizontal dilations of logarithmic functions become vertical translations and dilations.
Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and powers into multiplication. Those two facts let you combine logarithmic terms into one, which is exactly what free-response Question 4 asks for.
Topic 2.4 rewrote exponential expressions with the properties of exponents. Each property of logarithms here is the same property read through the inverse relationship of Topic 2.10.
records.excerpt: The product, power, and change of base properties for logarithms, the natural logarithm, and how horizontal dilations of logarithmic functions become vertical translations and dilations.

records.title: Logarithmic Function Manipulation
records.heading: 2.12.A · The product property: a horizontal dilation is a vertical translation.
records.text:
2.12.A · The product property: a horizontal dilation is a vertical translation.
log_b (xy) = log_b x + log_b y, so log_b (kx) is log_b x shifted by log_b k.
The product property for logarithms states that log_b (xy) = log_b x + log_b y. Graphically, this property implies that every horizontal dilation of a logarithmic function, f(x) = log_b (kx), is equivalent to a vertical translation, f(x) = log_b (kx) = log_b k + log_b x = a + log_b x, where a = log_b k.
Example: log₂ (8x) = log₂ 8 + log₂ x = 3 + log₂ x. Compressing the graph of y = log₂ x horizontally by a factor of 1/8 gives the same graph as translating it up 3 units.
Combining the product property with the power property below gives a rule for quotients: log_b (x/y) = log_b (x·y⁻¹) = log_b x − log_b y. For example, log₂ 48 − log₂ 3 = log₂ 16 = 4.

records.title: Logarithmic Function Manipulation
records.heading: 2.12.A · Change of base: all logarithmic functions are vertical dilations of each other.
records.text:
2.12.A · Change of base: all logarithmic functions are vertical dilations of each other.
log_b x = (log_a x)/(log_a b), and ln x = logₑ x.
The change of base property for logarithms states that log_b x = (log_a x)/(log_a b), where a > 0 and a ≠ 1. This implies that all logarithmic functions are vertical dilations of each other.
The function f(x) = ln x is a logarithmic function with the natural base e; that is, ln x = logₑ x.
Example: log₅ 40 = (ln 40)/(ln 5) ≈ 2.292. Also log₈ x = (log₂ x)/(log₂ 8) = (1/3) log₂ x, so the graph of y = log₈ x is a vertical dilation of y = log₂ x by a factor of 1/3.

records.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
records.text:
Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
Solving exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities with properties and inverses, checking for extraneous solutions, rewriting exponential expressions with logarithms, and finding inverses of transformed exponential and logarithmic functions.
To solve for a variable in an exponent, take a logarithm; to solve for a variable inside a logarithm, exponentiate. Then check each answer, because the domain of a logarithm can rule some out.
Free-response Question 4 on the AP Exam asks you to solve exponential and logarithmic equations without a calculator and to show every step. This topic brings together the properties from Topics 2.4 and 2.12.
records.excerpt: Solving exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities with properties and inverses, checking for extraneous solutions, rewriting exponential expressions with logarithms, and finding inverses of transformed exponential and logarithmic functions.

records.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
records.heading: 2.13.A · Use properties and the inverse relationship to solve equations and inequalities.
records.text:
2.13.A · Use properties and the inverse relationship to solve equations and inequalities.
Exponent unknown: take a log. Log unknown: exponentiate. Decreasing functions reverse inequalities.
Properties of exponents, properties of logarithms, and the inverse relationship between exponential and logarithmic functions can be used to solve equations and inequalities involving exponents and logarithms.
Three kinds of equations
Equation
Method
Solution
3^(2x − 1) = 27
Common base: 27 = 3³, so 2x − 1 = 3
x = 2
4ˣ = 20
Take a logarithm: x = log₄ 20 = (ln 20)/(ln 4)
x ≈ 2.161
log₅ (x + 2) = 2
Exponentiate: x + 2 = 5²
x = 23
Inequalities follow the same steps, as long as the function applied to both sides preserves the order. Because 2ˣ is always increasing, 2ˣ > 32 = 2⁵ gives x > 5. Because (1/2)ˣ is always decreasing, (1/2)ˣ > 1/32 gives x < 5.
6e^(2x) − e = 2e. 6e^(2x) = 3e. e^(2x) = e/2. 2x = ln (e/2) = 1 − ln 2. x = (1 − ln 2)/2.

records.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
records.heading: 2.13.A · Check solutions for extraneous solutions.
records.text:
2.13.A · Check solutions for extraneous solutions.
Every argument of every logarithm must be positive at the solution.
When solving exponential and logarithmic equations found through analytical or graphical methods, the results should be examined for extraneous solutions precluded by the mathematical or contextual limitations.
Example: log₂ x + log₂ (x − 2) = 3. The product property gives log₂ (x(x − 2)) = 3, so x² − 2x = 8 and (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0. The value x = −2 is extraneous, because log₂ (−2) is undefined. The only solution is x = 4.
x = −2 is not a solution because −2 is not in the domain of log₂ x. Therefore x = 4.

records.heading: 2.13.A · Logarithms can rewrite exponential expressions.
records.text:
2.13.A · Logarithms can rewrite exponential expressions.
Any exponential can be rewritten with any other base: bˣ = c^((log_c b)x).
Logarithms can be used to rewrite expressions involving exponential functions in different ways that may reveal helpful information. Specifically, bˣ = c^((log_c b)(x)).
Example: 2ˣ = e^((ln 2)x) ≈ e^(0.693x). A model written with base e shows a continuous rate, while the same model written with base 2 shows a doubling.

records.heading: 2.13.B · Find inverses of transformed exponential and logarithmic functions.
records.text:
2.13.B · Find inverses of transformed exponential and logarithmic functions.
Undo k, then a, then the exponential or logarithm, then h.
The function f(x) = ab^(x + h) + k is a combination of additive transformations of an exponential function in general form. The inverse of y = f(x) can be found by determining the inverse operations to reverse the mapping.
The function f(x) = a log_b (x + h) + k is a combination of additive transformations of a logarithmic function in general form. The inverse of y = f(x) can be found by determining the inverse operations to reverse the mapping.
y = 5(2)^(x − 1) + 3. Reverse x and y: x = 5(2)^(y − 1) + 3. Then (x − 3)/5 = 2^(y − 1), so y − 1 = log₂ ((x − 3)/5) and f⁻¹(x) = log₂ ((x − 3)/5) + 1.

records.title: Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling
records.text:
Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling
When a logarithmic model fits, building one from a proportion and a zero or from two points, transformations and logarithmic regression, the natural logarithm in models, and using the model to predict and solve.
A logarithmic model fits when equal steps in the output come from multiplying the input by the same factor. Its output counts how many times the input has been multiplied by that factor.
Topic 2.5 modeled proportional growth in the outputs with exponential functions. Logarithmic functions model the reverse situation, where the inputs grow proportionally, as in sound levels, earthquake magnitudes, and pH.
records.excerpt: When a logarithmic model fits, building one from a proportion and a zero or from two points, transformations and logarithmic regression, the natural logarithm in models, and using the model to predict and solve.

records.title: Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 2.14.A · Logarithmic functions model proportional change in the inputs.
records.text:
2.14.A · Logarithmic functions model proportional change in the inputs.
Inputs multiply by a constant while outputs add a constant: logarithmic.
Logarithmic functions are inverses of exponential functions and can be used to model situations involving proportional growth, or repeated multiplication, where the input values change proportionally over equal-length output-value intervals. Alternately, if the output value is a whole number, it indicates how many times the initial value has been multiplied by the proportion.
A loudness rating L for sound sources of intensity I (relative units)
I
1
10
100
1,000
10,000
L
0
10
20
30
40
Each time the intensity is multiplied by 10, the rating increases by 10. The inputs change proportionally over equal-length output intervals, so L(I) = 10 log I is a logarithmic model. L = 30 says the intensity 1 has been multiplied by 10 three times.
The natural logarithm function is often useful in modeling real-world phenomena.

records.heading: 2.14.A · Build a model from a proportion and a zero, two points, transformations, or regression.
records.text:
2.14.A · Build a model from a proportion and a zero, two points, transformations, or regression.
Two points give two linear equations in a and b once the logarithms are evaluated.
A logarithmic function model can be constructed from an appropriate proportion and a real zero or from two input-output pairs.
Example: a model of the form y = a + b log₂ x passes through (2, 10) and (8, 16). Since log₂ 2 = 1 and log₂ 8 = 3, the system is a + b = 10 and a + 3b = 16. Subtracting gives 2b = 6, so b = 3 and a = 7. The model is y = 7 + 3 log₂ x.
Logarithmic function models can be constructed by applying transformations to f(x) = a log_b x based on characteristics of a context or data set.
Logarithmic function models can be constructed for a data set with technology using logarithmic regressions.
Using the given data, a + b log₂ 2 = 10 and a + b log₂ 8 = 16, so a + b = 10 and a + 3b = 16. Therefore b = 3 and a = 7.

records.heading: 2.14.A · Use the model to predict outputs and to find inputs.
records.text:
2.14.A · Use the model to predict outputs and to find inputs.
Predict by evaluating; find an input by exponentiating.
Logarithmic function models can be used to predict values for the dependent variable, and they may be used to determine values of the independent variable.
With y = 7 + 3 log₂ x, the prediction at x = 32 is 7 + 3(5) = 22. To find when y = 25, solve 3 log₂ x = 18, so log₂ x = 6 and x = 64.
In chemistry, pH = −log [H⁺]. A solution with [H⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ has pH = −log (3.2 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 3.495.

records.title: Semi-log Plots
records.text:
Semi-log Plots
Semi-log plots with a logarithmically scaled y-axis, why exponential data appear linear on them, and the linear model log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a that comes from y = abˣ.
Taking a logarithm of exponential outputs turns multiplication into addition, so exponential data line up along a straight line. A straight semi-log plot is evidence for an exponential model.
Topic 2.6 judged models with residuals, and Topic 2.12 showed that logarithms turn products into sums. A semi-log plot combines the two ideas into a quick visual test for exponential data.
records.excerpt: Semi-log plots with a logarithmically scaled y-axis, why exponential data appear linear on them, and the linear model log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a that comes from y = abˣ.

records.heading: 2.15.A · On a semi-log plot, exponential data appear linear.
records.text:
2.15.A · On a semi-log plot, exponential data appear linear.
Linear on a semi-log plot (log of y against x) means exponential.
In a semi-log plot, one of the axes is logarithmically scaled with logarithm base n, where n > 1. When the y-axis of a semi-log plot is logarithmically scaled, data or functions that demonstrate exponential characteristics will appear linear.

Semi-log plot of the data: log y against x lies on a line with slope log 3 ≈ 0.477
If for large input values of a bivariate data set the logarithms of the output values trend linear, then transformations of an exponential function can be used to model the data set. Therefore, an advantage of semi-log plots is that the dependent variable values do not need to be transformed by a constant to reveal that transformations of an exponential function would produce an appropriate model.
An exponential model is appropriate because the semi-log plot of the data, with log y on the vertical axis, appears linear.

records.title: Semi-log Plots
records.heading: 2.15.B · y = abˣ becomes the line log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a.
records.text:
2.15.B · y = abˣ becomes the line log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a.
Slope = log_n b, intercept = log_n a. Undo with n^(slope) and n^(intercept).
Techniques used to model linear functions can be applied to a semi-log graph.
For an exponential model of the form y = abˣ, the corresponding linear model for the semi-log plot is y = (log_n b)x + log_n a, where n > 0 and n ≠ 1. Specifically, the linear rate of change is log_n b, and the initial linear value is log_n a.
Here the vertical coordinate of the semi-log plot is log_n of the original output. For y = 2(3)ˣ with n = 10, the line has slope log 3 ≈ 0.477 and vertical intercept log 2 ≈ 0.301.
The process also runs backward. If a semi-log plot with base 10 has the line log y = 0.5x + 1, then log b = 0.5 and log a = 1, so b = 10^0.5 ≈ 3.162 and a = 10, and y ≈ 10(3.162)ˣ.
Taking log of both sides of y = abˣ gives log y = log a + x log b, which is linear in x with slope log b and intercept log a.
records.excerpt: Slope = log_n b, intercept = log_n a. Undo with n^(slope) and n^(intercept).

records.title: Periodic Phenomena
records.text:
Periodic Phenomena
What makes a relationship periodic, how one cycle of a graph builds the whole graph, the period of a function, and estimating a period from data.
A periodic relationship repeats the same pattern of output values over and over. Once you know one full cycle, you know the whole function, because every characteristic of one period appears in every period.
Units 1 and 2 studied functions that rise or fall toward their end behavior. Unit 3 turns to functions that repeat: tides, rotating wheels, and sound waves. This topic sets up the vocabulary before the sine and cosine functions arrive in Topics 3.2 to 3.5.
records.excerpt: What makes a relationship periodic, how one cycle of a graph builds the whole graph, the period of a function, and estimating a period from data.

records.title: Periodic Phenomena
records.heading: 3.1.A · A periodic relationship repeats over successive equal-length intervals.
records.text:
3.1.A · A periodic relationship repeats over successive equal-length intervals.
Periodic means the output pattern repeats over equal-length input intervals; one cycle builds the whole graph.
A periodic relationship can be identified between two aspects of a context if, as the input values increase, the output values demonstrate a repeating pattern over successive equal-length intervals. The height of a seat on a turning Ferris wheel, the water level at a harbor over several days, and the position of a swinging pendulum are all periodic.
The graph of a periodic relationship can be constructed from the graph of a single cycle of the relationship. Draw one cycle, then copy it end to end in both directions.
Example: a windshield wiper sweeps at a constant rate from the bottom of the windshield up to 90° in 1 second, then back down to 0° in the next second, and repeats. Let W(t) be the wiper's angle, in degrees, t seconds after it starts. One cycle is the rise from (0, 0) to (1, 90) and the fall back to (2, 0). The graph below repeats that single cycle.
The wiper angle W(t), built from copies of one 2-second cycle
The wiper graph is made of line segments, yet it is periodic because the same pattern repeats over intervals of equal length. Sinusoidal functions, which start in Topic 3.5, are the smooth periodic functions this unit focuses on.

records.title: Periodic Phenomena
records.heading: 3.1.B · The period is the length of the shortest interval that repeats.
records.text:
3.1.B · The period is the length of the shortest interval that repeats.
Smallest k with f(x + k) = f(x); whatever happens in one period happens in every period.
The period of the function is the smallest positive value k such that f(x + k) = f(x) for all x in the domain. Consequently, the behavior of a periodic function is completely determined by any interval of width k.
For the wiper, W(t + 2) = W(t) for every t, and no smaller positive number works, so the period is 2 seconds. It is also true that W(t + 4) = W(t), but 4 is not the smallest such value.
The period can be estimated by investigating successive equal-length output values and finding where the pattern begins to repeat. A single repeated output is not enough: the whole sequence of outputs has to start over.
Water depth D(t), in feet, at a dock, t hours after midnight

D(t)

The depth returns to 8 feet at t = 6, but the next value is 5, not 11, so the pattern has not started over. The full pattern 8, 11, 8, 5 begins again at t = 12, so the period is estimated to be 12 hours.
Periodic functions take on characteristics of other functions, such as intervals of increase and decrease, different concavities, and various rates of change. However, with periodic functions, all characteristics found in one period of the function will be in every period of the function.
Because W has period 2 and W is increasing on 0 < t < 1, W is also increasing on 2 < t < 3, 4 < t < 5, and every interval 2n < t < 2n + 1 for integers n.

records.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
records.text:
Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
Angles in standard position, terminal rays, radian measure, and the sine, cosine, and tangent of an angle defined from a point on a circle centered at the origin.
An angle in standard position picks out a terminal ray, and that ray meets any circle centered at the origin at a point P. Sine, cosine, and tangent are ratios built from P's coordinates and its distance from the origin.
Topic 3.1 described periodic relationships in general. To build periodic functions, this topic measures angles as rotations and defines three ratios that repeat every time the rotation completes a full turn.
records.excerpt: Angles in standard position, terminal rays, radian measure, and the sine, cosine, and tangent of an angle defined from a point on a circle centered at the origin.

records.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
records.heading: 3.2.A · Angles in standard position are measured in radians.
records.text:
3.2.A · Angles in standard position are measured in radians.
Radian measure is arc length over radius; angles that differ by whole revolutions share a terminal ray.
In the coordinate plane, an angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis. The other ray is called the terminal ray. Positive and negative angle measures indicate rotations from the positive x-axis in the counterclockwise and clockwise direction, respectively. Angles in standard position that share a terminal ray differ by an integer number of revolutions.
When considering a circle centered at the origin, the radian measure of an angle in standard position is the ratio of the length of the arc of the circle that the angle subtends to the radius of that same circle. For a unit circle, which has radius 1, one radian is the measure of the angle subtended at the center of the circle by an arc that has length 1.
An angle of 2π/3 in standard position, with its terminal ray meeting the unit circle at P
A full revolution subtends the whole circumference, 2πr, so it measures 2πr/r = 2π radians. Half a revolution is π, and a quarter revolution is π/2. The angles 2π/3, 2π/3 + 2π = 8π/3, and 2π/3 − 2π = −4π/3 all share the terminal ray shown above.
Because the radian measure θ is arc length divided by radius, the arc length on a circle of radius r is s = rθ. A 2-radian angle on a circle of radius 30 cm subtends an arc of 60 cm.

records.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
records.heading: 3.2.A · Sine, cosine, and tangent come from the point where the terminal ray meets the circle.
records.text:
3.2.A · Sine, cosine, and tangent come from the point where the terminal ray meets the circle.
sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x; on the unit circle, P = (cos θ, sin θ).
Given an angle in standard position and a circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The sine of the angle is the ratio of the vertical displacement of P from the x-axis to the distance between the origin and point P. Therefore, for a unit circle, the sine of the angle is the y-coordinate of point P.
Given an angle in standard position and a circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The cosine of the angle is the ratio of the horizontal displacement of P from the y-axis to the distance between the origin and point P. Therefore, for a unit circle, the cosine of the angle is the x-coordinate of point P.
Given an angle in standard position, the tangent of the angle is the slope, if it exists, of the terminal ray. Because the slope of the terminal ray is the ratio of the vertical displacement to the horizontal displacement over any interval, the tangent of the angle is the ratio of the y-coordinate to the x-coordinate of the point at which the terminal ray intersects the unit circle; alternately, it is the ratio of the angle's sine to its cosine.
The terminal ray of θ passes through P(−3, 4) on a circle of radius 5
Example: P is 5 units from the origin, since √((−3)² + 4²) = 5. So sin θ = 4/5, cos θ = −3/5, and tan θ = 4/(−3) = −4/3. The tangent is also (4/5)/(−3/5) = −4/3, the ratio of the sine to the cosine.

If the terminal ray lies on the y-axis, as for θ = π/2, the ray is vertical, its slope does not exist, and tan θ is undefined. In that case cos θ = 0, so sin θ/cos θ is undefined too.

records.title: Sine and Cosine Function Values
records.text:
Sine and Cosine Function Values
The coordinates (r cos θ, r sin θ) of a point on a circle centered at the origin, and exact sine and cosine values for multiples of π/4 and π/6 from special right triangles.
Every point on a circle of radius r centered at the origin can be written as (r cos θ, r sin θ). For angles that are multiples of π/4 and π/6, two special triangles give the exact values of the cosine and sine, and the quadrant gives their signs.
Topic 3.2 defined sine and cosine as ratios. This topic turns the ratios around to find coordinates, and builds the exact values that AP Exam questions without a calculator expect.
records.excerpt: The coordinates (r cos θ, r sin θ) of a point on a circle centered at the origin, and exact sine and cosine values for multiples of π/4 and π/6 from special right triangles.

records.title: Sine and Cosine Function Values
records.heading: 3.3.A · A point on a circle of radius r has coordinates (r cos θ, r sin θ).
records.text:
3.3.A · A point on a circle of radius r has coordinates (r cos θ, r sin θ).
x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a circle with radius r centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The coordinates of point P are (r cos θ, r sin θ).
This follows from Topic 3.2: cos θ = x/r and sin θ = y/r, so x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
Example: on a circle of radius 6, the terminal ray of θ = 5π/6 meets the circle at (6 cos(5π/6), 6 sin(5π/6)) = (6(−√3/2), 6(1/2)) = (−3√3, 3).
A Ferris wheel of radius 20 meters has its center 25 meters above the ground. A seat that starts level with the center, on the right side, and turns counterclockwise through an angle θ is 20 sin θ meters above the center, so its height is 25 + 20 sin θ meters. After θ = π/6 the seat is 25 + 20(1/2) = 35 meters high.

records.text:
3.3.A · Special triangles give exact values for multiples of π/4 and π/6.
Use the triangle for the size of the value and the quadrant for its sign.
The geometry of isosceles right and equilateral triangles, while attending to the signs of the values based on the quadrant of the angle, can be used to find exact values for the cosine and sine of angles that are multiples of π/4 and π/6 radians and whose terminal rays do not lie on an axis.
An isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse 1 has legs √2/2, which gives the values at π/4. Cutting an equilateral triangle with side 1 in half gives legs 1/2 and √3/2, which gives the values at π/6 and π/3.

records.title: Sine and Cosine Function Graphs
records.text:
Sine and Cosine Function Graphs
The sine and cosine functions as the vertical and horizontal displacements of a point moving around the unit circle, their domains, their outputs between −1 and 1, and how to sketch their graphs.
As an angle θ grows, the point P where its terminal ray meets the unit circle travels around and around. Plotting P's y-coordinate against θ gives the graph of sine; plotting its x-coordinate gives the graph of cosine.
Topics 3.2 and 3.3 found sine and cosine one angle at a time. This topic treats them as functions of θ and turns the unit circle into the two graphs used for the rest of the unit.

3.4.A · The cosine function gives the horizontal displacement of P from the y-axis.
cos θ is P's horizontal position; sine and cosine have the same shape, a quarter turn apart.
Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a unit circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The cosine function, f(θ) = cos θ, gives the x-coordinate, or horizontal displacement from the y-axis, of point P. The domain of the cosine function is all real numbers.
As the input values, or angle measures, of the cosine function increase, the output values oscillate between −1 and 1, taking every value in between and tracking the horizontal displacement of points on the unit circle from the y-axis.
y = cos θ (solid) and y = sin θ (dashed)
Example: as θ increases from π to 3π/2, P moves from (−1, 0) to (0, −1). Its x-coordinate goes from −1 to 0, so cos θ increases, while its y-coordinate goes from 0 to −1, so sin θ decreases.
On 0 < θ < π/2, cos θ is decreasing because P moves toward the y-axis, so its horizontal displacement from the y-axis shrinks from 1 to 0.

records.title: Sinusoidal Functions
records.text:
Sinusoidal Functions
Sinusoidal functions as transformations of sin θ, with period, frequency, amplitude, and midline, plus the concavity of their graphs and the symmetry that makes sine odd and cosine even.
Every sinusoidal function is a stretched and shifted copy of the sine graph. Four numbers describe it: the period, its reciprocal the frequency, the amplitude, and the midline.
Topic 3.4 drew the graphs of sine and cosine. This topic gives the vocabulary for their features, which Topic 3.6 then changes with transformations and Topic 3.7 uses to build models.
records.excerpt: Sinusoidal functions as transformations of sin θ, with period, frequency, amplitude, and midline, plus the concavity of their graphs and the symmetry that makes sine odd and cosine even.

records.title: Sinusoidal Functions
records.heading: 3.5.A · Sine and cosine are both sinusoidal functions.
records.text:
3.5.A · Sine and cosine are both sinusoidal functions.
Frequency = 1/period; for sin θ and cos θ the period is 2π.
A sinusoidal function is any function that involves additive and multiplicative transformations of f(θ) = sin θ. The sine and cosine functions are both sinusoidal functions, with cos θ = sin(θ + π/2).
The equation cos θ = sin(θ + π/2) says the cosine graph is the sine graph slid π/2 units to the left. In Topic 3.4, cosine reached its maximum at θ = 0, a quarter period before sine reached its maximum at θ = π/2.
The period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals. The period of f(θ) = sin θ and g(θ) = cos θ is 2π, and the frequency is 1/(2π).
The period is the length of one cycle; the frequency is the number of cycles per unit of input. A wave with period 1/4 second completes 4 cycles each second, so its frequency is 4 cycles per second.
records.excerpt: Frequency = 1/period; for sin θ and cos θ the period is 2π.

records.title: Sinusoidal Functions
records.heading: 3.5.A · Amplitude and midline come from the maximum and minimum.
records.text:
3.5.A · Amplitude and midline come from the maximum and minimum.
Amplitude = (max − min)/2; midline y = (max + min)/2.
The amplitude of a sinusoidal function is half the difference between its maximum and minimum values. The amplitude of f(θ) = sin θ and g(θ) = cos θ is 1.
The midline of the graph of a sinusoidal function is determined by the average, or arithmetic mean, of the maximum and minimum values of the function. The midline of the graphs of y = sin θ and y = cos θ is y = 0.
A sinusoidal function with maximum 9 and minimum 1
Example: for the function graphed above, the amplitude is (9 − 1)/2 = 4 and the midline is y = (9 + 1)/2 = 5. The dashed line marks the midline; the graph rises 4 units above it and falls 4 units below it.

records.title: Sinusoidal Functions
records.heading: 3.5.A · Concavity alternates, sine is odd, and cosine is even.
records.text:
3.5.A · Concavity alternates, sine is odd, and cosine is even.
Above the midline: concave down. Below: concave up. Sine is odd; cosine is even.
As input values increase, the graphs of sinusoidal functions oscillate between concave down and concave up.
For y = sin θ, the graph is concave down on 0 < θ < π, where it lies above its midline, and concave up on π < θ < 2π, where it lies below. The points of inflection are where the graph crosses the midline.
The graph of y = sin θ has rotational symmetry about the origin and is therefore an odd function. The graph of y = cos θ has reflective symmetry over the y-axis and is therefore an even function.

The graph of y = cos θ is concave up on π/2 < θ < 3π/2 because it is below its midline there; it changes concavity at θ = π/2 and θ = 3π/2, where it crosses the midline.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Transformations
records.text:
Sinusoidal Function Transformations
How a, b, c, and d in f(θ) = a sin(b(θ + c)) + d set the amplitude, period, phase shift, and midline of a sinusoidal function, for both sine and cosine.
Every sinusoidal function can be written as a sin(b(θ + c)) + d. Each parameter controls one feature: |a| the amplitude, |1/b|·2π the period, −c the phase shift, and d the midline.
Topic 1.12 transformed functions in general, and Topic 3.5 named the features of sinusoidal graphs. This topic connects the two, so you can read the features from an equation and write an equation from the features.
records.excerpt: How a, b, c, and d in f(θ) = a sin(b(θ + c)) + d set the amplitude, period, phase shift, and midline of a sinusoidal function, for both sine and cosine.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Transformations
records.heading: 3.6.A · Adding d moves the midline; adding c inside shifts the phase.
records.text:
3.6.A · Adding d moves the midline; adding c inside shifts the phase.
+d moves the graph up d; +c inside moves it −c units horizontally.
Functions that can be written in the form f(θ) = a sin(b(θ + c)) + d or g(θ) = a cos(b(θ + c)) + d, where a, b, c, and d are real numbers, a ≠ 0, and b ≠ 0, are sinusoidal functions and are transformations of the sine and cosine functions. Additive and multiplicative transformations are the same for both sine and cosine because the cosine function is a phase shift of the sine function by −π/2 units.
The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = sin θ + d of the sine function f(θ) = sin θ is a vertical translation of the graph of f, including its midline, by d units. The same transformation of the cosine function yields the same result.
The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = sin(θ + c) of the sine function f(θ) = sin θ is a horizontal translation, or phase shift, of the graph of f by −c units. The same transformation of the cosine function yields the same result.
Example: g(θ) = cos(θ − π/3) has c = −π/3, so its graph is the graph of y = cos θ shifted −c = π/3 units, which is π/3 units to the right. Its maximum moves from θ = 0 to θ = π/3.
records.excerpt: +d moves the graph up d; +c inside moves it −c units horizontally.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Transformations
records.heading: 3.6.A · Multiplying by a changes the amplitude; multiplying θ by b changes the period.
records.text:
3.6.A · Multiplying by a changes the amplitude; multiplying θ by b changes the period.
Amplitude |a|; period 2π/|b|.
The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = a sin θ of the sine function f(θ) = sin θ is a vertical dilation of the graph of f and differs in amplitude by a factor of |a|. The same transformation of the cosine function yields the same result.
The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = sin(bθ) of the sine function f(θ) = sin θ is a horizontal dilation of the graph of f and differs in period by a factor of |1/b|. The same transformation of the cosine function yields the same result.
y = sin θ (dashed), y = 3 sin θ, and y = sin(2θ)
Example: y = 3 sin θ has amplitude 3|1| = 3. y = sin(2θ) has period |1/2|·2π = π, so it fits two cycles where y = sin θ fits one. A negative a also reflects the graph over its midline, but the amplitude is still |a|.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
records.text:
Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
Building sinusoidal models of periodic phenomena: the period from consecutive maximums or minimums, the amplitude and midline from the extreme values, the phase shift from one data point, sinusoidal regression, and where a model can be trusted.
A sinusoidal model needs four numbers, and data supply each one: the time between peaks gives the period, the peak and trough give the amplitude and midline, and one known point fixes the phase shift.
Topic 3.6 read features from an equation. Here the direction reverses: start from a context or a table, estimate the features, and write the equation, by hand or with a regression.
records.excerpt: Building sinusoidal models of periodic phenomena: the period from consecutive maximums or minimums, the amplitude and midline from the extreme values, the phase shift from one data point, sinusoidal regression, and where a model can be trusted.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 3.7.A · Period from consecutive extremes; amplitude and midline from the extreme values.
records.text:
3.7.A · Period from consecutive extremes; amplitude and midline from the extreme values.
Peak to peak is a period; peak to trough is half a period.
The smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output values start to repeat, that is, the input-value interval between consecutive maxima or consecutive minima, can be used to determine or estimate the period and frequency for a sinusoidal function model.
The maximum and minimum output values can be used to determine or estimate the amplitude and vertical shift for a sinusoidal function model.
Example: at a harbor, high tide is 9.2 feet at 3:00 a.m. and the next low tide is 1.4 feet at 9:15 a.m. From a maximum to the next minimum is half a cycle, 6.25 hours, so the period is 12.5 hours and the frequency is 1/12.5 = 0.08 cycle per hour. The amplitude is (9.2 − 1.4)/2 = 3.9 feet and the midline is D = (9.2 + 1.4)/2 = 5.3 feet.

records.title: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
records.heading: 3.7.A · One data point fixes the phase shift; technology can do the fitting.
records.text:
3.7.A · One data point fixes the phase shift; technology can do the fitting.
Match one real point to fix c; trust the model mainly inside the data's domain.
An actual pair of input-output values can be compared to pairs of input-output values produced by a sinusoidal function model to determine or estimate a phase shift for the model.
For the tide, t is hours after midnight. Cosine reaches its maximum when its input is 0, and the real maximum is at t = 3, so the model needs b(t + c) = 0 at t = 3, which means c = −3. The model is D(t) = 3.9 cos(0.16π(t − 3)) + 5.3. Check: D(3) = 3.9 + 5.3 = 9.2 and D(9.25) = −3.9 + 5.3 = 1.4.
The tide model D(t) = 3.9 cos(0.16π(t − 3)) + 5.3 for the first day
Sinusoidal function models can be constructed for a data set with technology by estimating key values or using sinusoidal regressions. The calculator on this site fits y = a sin(b(x + c)) + d to a list of points; check its period and midline against the data before using it.
Sinusoidal functions that model a data set are frequently only useful over their contextual domain, can be used to predict values of the dependent variable from values of the independent variable, and may be used to determine values of the independent variable from values of the dependent variable.
Based on the model, the depth is predicted to be D(6) ≈ 5.54 feet at 6:00 a.m. Because the model was built from one day of tides, it is less reliable for predictions weeks later, when the times of high and low tide drift.

records.title: The Tangent Function
records.text:
The Tangent Function
The tangent function as the slope of the terminal ray, its period of π, its vertical asymptotes, its increasing and changing concavity between asymptotes, and its additive and multiplicative transformations.
The tangent function gives the slope of the terminal ray. The slope repeats every half turn and does not exist when the ray is vertical, so tangent has period π and a vertical asymptote every π units.
Topic 3.2 defined the tangent of a single angle. This topic graphs it as a function and transforms it, using the same a, b, c, and d as the sinusoidal functions in Topic 3.6.
records.excerpt: The tangent function as the slope of the terminal ray, its period of π, its vertical asymptotes, its increasing and changing concavity between asymptotes, and its additive and multiplicative transformations.

records.title: The Tangent Function
records.heading: 3.8.A · The tangent function gives the slope of the terminal ray.
records.text:
3.8.A · The tangent function gives the slope of the terminal ray.
tan θ = slope of the terminal ray = sin θ/cos θ.
Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a unit circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The tangent function, f(θ) = tan θ, gives the slope of the terminal ray.
Because the slope of the terminal ray is the ratio of the change in the y-values to the change in the x-values between any two points on the ray, the tangent function is also the ratio of the sine function to the cosine function. Therefore, tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ), where cos θ ≠ 0.
Example: if sin θ = −3/5 and cos θ = 4/5, then tan θ = (−3/5)/(4/5) = −3/4. The terminal ray points down and to the right, so its slope is negative.
records.excerpt: tan θ = slope of the terminal ray = sin θ/cos θ.

records.title: The Tangent Function
records.heading: 3.8.B · Period π, asymptotes where cos θ = 0, always increasing between them.
records.text:
3.8.B · Period π, asymptotes where cos θ = 0, always increasing between them.
Period π; asymptotes at π/2 + kπ; zeros and inflection points at kπ.
Because the slope values of the terminal ray repeat every one-half revolution of the circle, the tangent function has a period of π.
The tangent function demonstrates periodic asymptotic behavior at input values θ = π/2 + kπ, for integer values of k, because cos θ = 0 at those values.
The tangent function increases and its graph changes from concave down to concave up between consecutive asymptotes.
y = tan θ with its vertical asymptotes at θ = ±π/2 and ±3π/2
On −π/2 < θ < π/2, tan θ is increasing; its graph is concave down for −π/2 < θ < 0 and concave up for 0 < θ < π/2, so (0, 0) is a point of inflection.

records.heading: 3.8.C · Transformations of tangent work like those of sine and cosine.
records.text:
3.8.C · Transformations of tangent work like those of sine and cosine.
Period π/|b|; no amplitude, because tangent is unbounded.
The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = tan θ + d of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a vertical translation of the graph of f and the line containing its points of inflection by d units.
The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = tan(θ + c) of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a horizontal translation, or phase shift, of the graph of f by −c units.
The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = a tan θ of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a vertical dilation of the graph of f by a factor of |a|. If a < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the x-axis.
The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = tan(bθ) of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a horizontal dilation of the graph of f and differs in period by a factor of |1/b|. If b < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the y-axis.
The graph of y = f(θ) = a tan(b(θ + c)) + d is a vertical dilation of the graph of y = tan θ by a factor of |a|, has a period of |1/b|π units, is a vertical shift of the line containing the points of inflection of the graph of y = tan θ by d units, and is a phase shift of −c units.
y = a tan(b(θ + c)) + d. Move the sliders to compare with y = tan θ (dashed).
Example: f(θ) = 3 tan(2θ) − 1 has period |1/2|π = π/2, and its points of inflection lie on y = −1. Its asymptotes are where 2θ = π/2 + kπ, that is, θ = π/4 + kπ/2.

records.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
records.text:
Inverse Trigonometric Functions
Arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent: why the trigonometric functions need restricted domains to be invertible, which domains are used, and how the output of an inverse trigonometric function is read as an angle.
An inverse trigonometric function takes a value of sine, cosine, or tangent and returns an angle. Because the original functions repeat, each inverse returns only the one angle that lies in an agreed restricted domain.
Topic 2.8 found inverses by switching inputs and outputs, and required the function to be one-to-one. Sine, cosine, and tangent are periodic, so this topic restricts them before inverting.
records.excerpt: Arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent: why the trigonometric functions need restricted domains to be invertible, which domains are used, and how the output of an inverse trigonometric function is read as an angle.

records.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
records.heading: 3.9.A · Inverse trigonometric functions switch inputs and outputs.
records.text:
3.9.A · Inverse trigonometric functions switch inputs and outputs.
arcsin, arccos, and arctan take a ratio and return an angle.
For inverse trigonometric functions, the input and output values are switched from their corresponding trigonometric functions, so the output value of an inverse trigonometric function is often interpreted as an angle measure and the input is a value in the range of the corresponding trigonometric function.
The inverse trigonometric functions are called arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent (also represented as sin⁻¹x, cos⁻¹x, and tan⁻¹x). Because the corresponding trigonometric functions are periodic, they are only invertible if they have restricted domains.
Example: sin(π/6) = 1/2, so arcsin(1/2) = π/6. The input 1/2 is a value of sine, and the output π/6 is an angle. The notation sin⁻¹x means the inverse function, not 1/sin x.
A ramp rises 1.2 meters over a horizontal run of 6 meters, so the slope is tan θ = 0.2. The angle the ramp makes with the ground is θ = arctan(0.2) ≈ 0.197 radian.

records.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
records.text:
Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
Solving equations and inequalities involving trigonometric functions: one solution from an inverse function, the others from symmetry and periodicity, and the domain restrictions that a context implies.
An inverse trigonometric function returns one solution, chosen from its restricted range. The symmetry of the unit circle gives a second solution in each period, periodicity gives all the rest, and a context usually tells you which ones matter.
Topic 3.9 defined arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent. This topic uses them to solve equations such as sin θ = 0.3, then uses graphs to solve inequalities such as sin θ > 1/2.
records.excerpt: Solving equations and inequalities involving trigonometric functions: one solution from an inverse function, the others from symmetry and periodicity, and the domain restrictions that a context implies.

records.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
records.heading: 3.10.A · Inverses give one solution; periodicity gives infinitely many.
records.text:
3.10.A · Inverses give one solution; periodicity gives infinitely many.
One solution from the inverse, a second from symmetry, the rest by adding periods.
Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving equations and inequalities involving trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain restrictions.
Because trigonometric functions are periodic, there are often infinitely many solutions to trigonometric equations.
Example: solve 2 sin θ − 1 = 0. Then sin θ = 1/2, and arcsin(1/2) = π/6. Sine is also 1/2 in Quadrant II, at π − π/6 = 5π/6. On 0 ≤ θ < 2π the solutions are π/6 and 5π/6. Over all real numbers they are θ = π/6 + 2kπ and θ = 5π/6 + 2kπ for integers k.
The solutions of sin θ = 1/2 are where y = sin θ meets y = 1/2

records.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
records.heading: 3.10.A · Inequalities and contexts limit which solutions count.
records.text:
3.10.A · Inequalities and contexts limit which solutions count.
Solve the equation, read the inequality from the graph, and keep only solutions in the context's domain.
To solve an inequality such as sin θ > 1/2 on 0 ≤ θ < 2π, first solve the equation sin θ = 1/2, then use the graph to see where the curve is above the line. In the graph above, y = sin θ is above y = 1/2 between π/6 and 5π/6, so the solution is π/6 < θ < 5π/6.
In trigonometric equations and inequalities arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of solutions.
Example: a Ferris wheel rider's height is h(t) = 25 − 20 cos((π/4)t) meters, t minutes after boarding, during one 8-minute ride, 0 ≤ t ≤ 8. When is the rider higher than 35 meters? Solve 25 − 20 cos((π/4)t) > 35, which means cos((π/4)t) < −1/2. On 0 ≤ (π/4)t ≤ 2π, that happens for 2π/3 < (π/4)t < 4π/3, so 8/3 < t < 16/3. The rider is above 35 meters for 16/3 − 8/3 = 8/3, about 2.67 minutes.
Because the ride lasts 8 minutes, only solutions with 0 ≤ t ≤ 8 are in the domain of the model, so the rider is above 35 meters only for 8/3 < t < 16/3.

records.title: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions
records.text:
The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions
Secant, cosecant, and cotangent as reciprocals of cosine, sine, and tangent: where they are defined, their vertical asymptotes, their ranges, and the shapes of their graphs.
Each of the three new functions is 1 divided by a familiar one. Wherever the familiar function is 0, its reciprocal has a vertical asymptote, and wherever the familiar function is small, its reciprocal is large.
Topic 3.8 wrote tangent as the quotient sin θ/cos θ. This topic completes the set of quotients of sine and cosine, which Topic 3.12 then uses in identities.
records.excerpt: Secant, cosecant, and cotangent as reciprocals of cosine, sine, and tangent: where they are defined, their vertical asymptotes, their ranges, and the shapes of their graphs.

records.title: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions
records.heading: 3.11.A · Secant and cosecant are reciprocals of cosine and sine.
records.text:
3.11.A · Secant and cosecant are reciprocals of cosine and sine.
sec θ = 1/cos θ and csc θ = 1/sin θ; their outputs are never between −1 and 1.
The secant function, f(θ) = sec θ, is the reciprocal of the cosine function, where cos θ ≠ 0.
The cosecant function, f(θ) = csc θ, is the reciprocal of the sine function, where sin θ ≠ 0.
The graphs of the secant and cosecant functions have vertical asymptotes where cosine and sine are zero, respectively, and have a range of (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞).
y = sec θ with y = cos θ (dashed)
Example: cos(π/3) = 1/2, so sec(π/3) = 2. sin(7π/6) = −1/2, so csc(7π/6) = −2. Where cos θ = ±1, sec θ = ±1 too, which is why the branches of the secant graph touch the cosine graph at its maximums and minimums.

The cotangent function, f(θ) = cot θ, is the reciprocal of the tangent function, where tan θ ≠ 0. Equivalently, cot θ = (cos θ)/(sin θ), where sin θ ≠ 0.
The graph of the cotangent function has vertical asymptotes for domain values where tan θ = 0 and is decreasing between consecutive asymptotes.

records.title: Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions
records.text:
Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions
The Pythagorean identity and forms derived from it, the sum identities for sine and cosine with their difference and double-angle versions, and using equivalent forms to solve trigonometric equations.
An identity is an equation that is true for every input where both sides are defined, so it lets you trade one expression for another. Choosing the right form turns an unfamiliar equation into one you already know how to solve.
Topics 3.10 and 3.11 solved equations in a single trigonometric function. Equations that mix sine and cosine, or involve sums of angles, need identities first. The AP Exam's symbolic manipulation question asks for exactly this kind of rewriting.
records.excerpt: The Pythagorean identity and forms derived from it, the sum identities for sine and cosine with their difference and double-angle versions, and using equivalent forms to solve trigonometric equations.

records.title: Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions
records.heading: 3.12.A · The Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
records.text:
3.12.A · The Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and tan²θ = sec²θ − 1; the quadrant picks the sign.
The Pythagorean Theorem can be applied to right triangles with points on the unit circle at coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), resulting in the Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
The Pythagorean identity can be algebraically manipulated into other forms involving trigonometric functions, such as tan²θ = sec²θ − 1, and can be used to establish other trigonometric relationships, such as arcsin x = arccos(√(1 − x²)), with appropriate domain restrictions.
Dividing sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ gives tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, which is tan²θ = sec²θ − 1 wherever cos θ ≠ 0. The relationship arcsin x = arccos(√(1 − x²)) holds for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, where both sides name the same Quadrant I angle; for negative x, arcsin x is negative but arccosine never is.
Example: sin θ = 0.6 and the terminal ray of θ is in Quadrant II. Then cos²θ = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64, so cos θ = ±0.8, and the quadrant makes it −0.8.
Solving sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for cos θ gives two values, ±√(1 − sin²θ). The quadrant of θ chooses between them.

records.heading: 3.12.B · Sum identities for sine and cosine.
records.text:
3.12.B · Sum identities for sine and cosine.
Learn the two sum identities; differences and doubles follow from them.
The sum identity for sine is sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β.
The sum identity for cosine is cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β.
The sum identities for sine and cosine can also be used as difference and double-angle identities.
Identities that follow from the sum identities
Replace
Sine
Cosine
β with −β
sin(α − β) = sin α cos β − cos α sin β
cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β
β with α
sin(2α) = 2 sin α cos α
cos(2α) = cos²α − sin²α
Example: π/12 = π/3 − π/4, so cos(π/12) = cos(π/3)cos(π/4) + sin(π/3)sin(π/4) = (1/2)(√2/2) + (√3/2)(√2/2) = (√2 + √6)/4 ≈ 0.966.
Properties of trigonometric functions, known trigonometric identities, and other algebraic properties can be used to verify additional trigonometric identities. For instance, using the Pythagorean identity, cos(2α) = cos²α − sin²α can also be written as 1 − 2 sin²α or 2 cos²α − 1.

records.heading: 3.12.C · Rewrite to solve.
records.text:
3.12.C · Rewrite to solve.
Use an identity to get a single trigonometric function, then solve as in Topic 3.10.
A specific equivalent form involving trigonometric expressions can make information more accessible.
Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric equations and inequalities.
Example: solve 2 cos²θ + 3 sin θ − 3 = 0 on 0 ≤ θ < 2π. Replace cos²θ with 1 − sin²θ: 2 − 2 sin²θ + 3 sin θ − 3 = 0, so 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0. This factors as (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0, so sin θ = 1/2 or sin θ = 1. The solutions are θ = π/6, π/2, and 5π/6.
Rewrite so the equation has only one trigonometric function, solve that function for its values, then find every angle in the required interval.

records.title: Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
records.text:
Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
The polar coordinate system, polar coordinates (r, θ) with positive and negative r, converting between polar and rectangular coordinates, and locating complex numbers with either system.
A point can be located by how far right and up it is, (x, y), or by which direction it lies in and how far along that direction, (r, θ). Sine and cosine translate between the two descriptions.
Topic 3.3 found the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) on a circle of radius r. Polar coordinates name that point directly as (r, θ), and Topics 3.14 and 3.15 graph functions in this system.
records.excerpt: The polar coordinate system, polar coordinates (r, θ) with positive and negative r, converting between polar and rectangular coordinates, and locating complex numbers with either system.

records.title: Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
records.heading: 3.13.A · Polar coordinates give a direction and a signed distance.
records.text:
3.13.A · Polar coordinates give a direction and a signed distance.
θ picks the line; the sign of r picks the direction along it.
The polar coordinate system is based on a grid of circles centered at the origin and on lines through the origin. The positive x-axis is called the polar axis. Polar coordinates of a point are defined as an ordered pair, (r, θ). The value of θ is given by the measure of an angle in standard position whose terminal ray lies in a line that passes through the point, and r is the radial displacement of the point from the origin.
Positive values of r indicate radial displacement from the origin along the terminal ray of the angle θ. Negative values of r indicate radial displacement from the origin along the line containing the terminal ray of the angle θ, but in the opposite direction of the terminal ray of the angle θ. In the polar coordinate system, the same point can be represented many ways with combinations of positive and negative values of r and θ.
Points A(3, π/4) and B(−2, π/3) on a polar grid
B is on the line through the ray θ = π/3, but r = −2 places it 2 units in the opposite direction. The same point B is also (2, 4π/3), (2, −2π/3), and (−2, π/3 + 2π).
records.excerpt: θ picks the line; the sign of r picks the direction along it.

records.heading: 3.13.A · Converting between polar and rectangular coordinates.
records.text:
3.13.A · Converting between polar and rectangular coordinates.
x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ; r = √(x² + y²), θ = arctan(y/x), plus π when x < 0.
The coordinates of a point in the polar coordinate system, (r, θ), can be converted to coordinates in the rectangular coordinate system, (x, y), using x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
The coordinates of a point in the rectangular coordinate system, (x, y), can be converted to coordinates in the polar coordinate system, (r, θ), using r = √(x² + y²) and θ = arctan(y/x) for x > 0 or θ = arctan(y/x) + π for x < 0.

records.title: Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
records.heading: 3.13.A · Complex numbers are points in the complex plane.
records.text:
3.13.A · Complex numbers are points in the complex plane.
a + bi ↔ (a, b); (r, θ) ↔ (r cos θ) + i(r sin θ).
A complex number can be understood as a point in the complex plane and can be determined by its corresponding rectangular or polar coordinates. When the complex number has the rectangular coordinates (a, b), it can be expressed as a + bi. When the complex number has polar coordinates (r, θ), it can be expressed as (r cos θ) + i(r sin θ).
Example: z = 1 − √3 i is the point (1, −√3). Its distance from the origin is √(1 + 3) = 2, and since x > 0, θ = arctan(−√3) = −π/3. So z = 2 cos(−π/3) + i(2 sin(−π/3)), which can also be written with θ = 5π/3.

records.title: Polar Function Graphs
records.text:
Polar Function Graphs
Graphing r = f(θ) in polar coordinates: reading angle as direction and output as signed radius, connecting the rectangular graph of r against θ to the polar curve, and restricting the domain to draw part of a curve.
A polar function turns each angle into a distance. Sweep θ around the origin and move out (or back) by r = f(θ): circles, cardioids, and roses all come from that one rule.
Topic 3.13 plotted single points (r, θ). Here r depends on θ, so the points form a curve. The rectangular graph of r against θ is the best tool for predicting the polar picture.

records.text:
3.14.A · Input is an angle; output is a signed radius.
Sweep the angle, set the signed distance, and use the r–θ graph to predict the shape.
The graph of the function r = f(θ) in polar coordinates consists of input-output pairs of values where the input values are angle measures and the output values are radii.
When graphing polar functions in the form of r = f(θ), changes in input values relate to changes in angle measures from the polar axis, and changes in output values relate to changes in signed radial displacements from the origin.

Reading the two graphs together: as θ increases from 0 to π, r decreases from 4 to 0, so the curve sweeps counterclockwise while moving in toward the origin. From π to 2π, r increases back to 4.

For r = 3 sin(2θ), r = 0 at θ = 0 and θ = π/2 and r = 3 at θ = π/4, so 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 draws exactly the petal in Quadrant I. On π/2 < θ < π, sin(2θ) < 0, so r < 0 and those points land in the opposite quadrant, Quadrant IV.
For π/2 < θ < π, r = 3 sin(2θ) is negative, so the points of the graph are in Quadrant IV, opposite the terminal rays of θ in Quadrant II.

records.title: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
records.text:
Rates of Change in Polar Functions
When the graph of a polar function moves toward or away from the origin, relative extrema as points closest to or farthest from the origin, and the average rate of change of r with respect to θ.
The distance from the origin is |r|, so whether a polar curve moves away from the origin depends on both the sign of r and whether r is increasing or decreasing. The average rate of change of r measures how fast the signed radius changes per radian.
Topic 3.14 drew polar graphs. This topic describes how they change, in the same language Unit 1 used for functions: increasing, decreasing, extrema, and average rates of change.

records.title: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
records.heading: 3.15.A · The sign of r and its direction of change decide the distance.
records.text:
3.15.A · The sign of r and its direction of change decide the distance.
Same sign of r and its change: moving away. Opposite: moving closer.
If a polar function, r = f(θ), is positive and increasing or negative and decreasing, then the distance between the point with polar coordinates (f(θ), θ) and the origin is increasing.
If a polar function, r = f(θ), is positive and decreasing or negative and increasing, then the distance between the point with polar coordinates (f(θ), θ) and the origin is decreasing.
Is the point moving away from the origin?
r = f(θ) is
Increasing
Decreasing
Positive

Negative

Distance increasing
r = 1 + 2 cos θ graphed with θ on the horizontal axis
Example: for r = 1 + 2 cos θ on 0 < θ < π, r is decreasing. On 0 < θ < 2π/3, r is positive, so the distance from the origin is decreasing. On 2π/3 < θ < π, r is negative, so the distance is increasing: the curve is tracing its inner loop outward.
For a polar function, r = f(θ), if the function changes from increasing to decreasing or decreasing to increasing on an interval, then the function has a relative extremum on the interval corresponding to a point relatively closest to or farthest from the origin.
On 2π/3 < θ < π, the distance between the point (f(θ), θ) and the origin is increasing because f is negative and decreasing on that interval.

records.title: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
records.heading: 3.15.A · Average rate of change of r with respect to θ.
records.text:
3.15.A · Average rate of change of r with respect to θ.
Δr/Δθ: change in signed radius per radian, useful for estimates inside the interval.
The average rate of change of r with respect to θ over an interval of θ is the ratio of the change in the signed radius values to the change in θ over an interval of θ. Graphically, the average rate of change indicates the rate at which the signed radius is changing per radian.
The average rate of change of r with respect to θ over an interval of θ can be used to estimate values of the function within the interval.
Example: for r = 1 + 2 cos θ on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, the average rate of change is (f(π/2) − f(0))/(π/2 − 0) = (1 − 3)/(π/2) = −4/π ≈ −1.273. On average, the signed radius decreases by about 1.273 units per radian on this interval.
Estimating with it: f(π/4) ≈ f(0) + (−4/π)(π/4) = 3 − 1 = 2. The actual value is 1 + 2 cos(π/4) = 1 + √2 ≈ 2.414, so the estimate is reasonable but not exact, because r does not change at a constant rate.
The average rate of change of r with respect to θ is in units of radius per radian, the same kind of ratio as the average rates of change in Topic 1.2.
